card.title: Swiss AI governance
card.one_liner: Switzerland has no overarching AI-specific act yet; existing data-protection law applies to AI processing of personal data, while an AI-law consultation draft is planned for spring 2027.
card.who_it_hits: Private controllers and processors, federal bodies, and organisations that use AI to process personal data in Switzerland; separate cantonal rules may apply to cantonal and municipal bodies.
card.status_line: Binding FADP and Data Protection Ordinance duties apply today. The Federal Council reported a spring 2027 consultation for proposed AI legislation; OFCOM's AI Code of Conduct guide is voluntary.

instruments.notes: Technology-neutral data protection law, not an AI Act. Fedlex English text is an informational translation.

card.title: China AI Governance Rules
card.one_liner: China regulates public-facing AI through service-specific filing, safety, data, user-protection and AI-content-labelling rules.
card.who_it_hits: Providers of algorithmic recommendation, deep-synthesis, generative AI and human-like interactive services in China, plus content-distribution and app-distribution platforms; each rule has its own scope.
card.status_line: Binding rules apply. GB 45438-2025 and the content-labelling measures apply from 1 Sep 2025; the amended Cybersecurity Law applies from 1 Jan 2026; human-like interactive-service rules apply from 15 Jul 2026. Comprehensive AI legislation remains a proposed work-plan item.

card.title: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention (CETS No. 225)
card.one_liner: A human-rights treaty requiring its Parties to govern AI lifecycle activities through safeguards, transparency, oversight, remedies and risk management.
card.who_it_hits: Treaty Parties must implement the Convention for public authorities and private actors acting on their behalf; each Party chooses how to address other private actors under Article 3.
card.status_line: Treaty, not yet in force as of 4 November 2026. The EU and Bosnia and Herzegovina have ratified; Article 30(3) requires five consents including three Council of Europe member States, followed by three months.

card.title: EU AI Act (as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI)
card.one_liner: The world's first horizontal AI law. Bans some uses, sets transparency duties for chatbots and generated content, and adds strict rules for high-risk systems.
card.who_it_hits: Anyone who places an AI system or general-purpose AI model on the EU market, or uses AI in the EU, wherever the company is based.
card.status_line: Binding. Bans since 2 Feb 2025, GPAI rules since 2 Aug 2025, transparency since 2 Aug 2026. Next dates are 2 Dec 2026 (new bans, marking for existing systems) and 2 Dec 2027 (Annex III high-risk).

card.title: UK AI regulation
card.one_liner: No general cross-sector AI Act; existing data, online-safety and criminal laws apply through sector regulators.
card.who_it_hits: AI developers and deployers, controllers making significant automated decisions, in-scope online services, and public bodies using algorithmic tools.
card.status_line: Binding UK GDPR ADM safeguards apply from 5 February 2026. Online-safety duties cover specified services, not every standalone chatbot. England-and-Wales intimate-image offences are in force; Scotland child-image-generator provisions are enacted but not commenced. The ATRS is a mandatory government policy for specified central bodies, not a statute.

obligations.title: Process personal data transparently and build privacy in by design
obligations.plain: Personal data must be processed lawfully, in good faith and proportionately; the purpose must be recognisable to the data subject and further processing must remain compatible with that purpose. Controllers must design processing to respect these principles from the planning stage and use suitable default settings to limit data to what is necessary.

applies_to.conditions: Applies when AI processing concerns personal data of natural persons and the organisation is a private person or federal body within the FADP's scope.

evidence: Purpose and lawful-basis records for AI-related personal-data processing
Privacy-by-design review and data-minimising default settings

obligations.title: Keep a record of processing activities
obligations.plain: Controllers and processors must keep records describing their processing activities, including purpose, data and data-subject categories, recipients, retention, security measures and relevant foreign disclosures. Natural persons and private organisations with fewer than 250 employees are generally exempt unless they process a large volume of sensitive personal data or carry out high-risk profiling; federal bodies must notify the FDPIC of their records.

applies_to.conditions: Record only processing of personal data; the small-organisation exception and its sensitive-data/high-risk-profiling limits are in DPO Art. 24.

evidence: Current processing inventory covering AI uses, data categories, purposes, recipients and transfers
Documented exemption analysis, if relying on the DPO Art. 24 exception

obligations.article: Art. 6(3), 19(1)–(2); FDPIC, AI and data protection, Transparent information
obligations.title: Tell people how AI processes their personal data
obligations.plain: Controllers must make the purpose of personal-data processing recognisable and inform data subjects appropriately when collecting personal data, including the controller's identity, processing purpose and, where applicable, recipients. The FDPIC says that AI providers and users should make purpose, functionality and data sources transparent; users of directly interactive language models should know they are communicating with a machine and how their prompts may be used.

applies_to.conditions: Only where personal data is processed within the FADP's scope; the FDPIC's AI-specific disclosure statement is its application of general FADP transparency duties, not a separate AI Act.

evidence: Notice describing the AI processing purpose, data sources, and prompt retention or reuse
User-facing disclosure when an interactive language model is a machine
obligations.notes: FDPIC's 2025 statement also says use of programs that manipulate identifiable persons' faces, images or voice messages must be clearly indicated. This is the regulator's interpretation of existing data-protection duties, not a standalone statutory deepfake-labelling article. See https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/ai-and-data-protection.
obligations.cite: Revised FADP Art. 6(3), 19(1)–(2); FDPIC, AI and data protection, Transparent information

obligations.title: Notify people about consequential decisions made solely by automation and offer human review
obligations.plain: If a decision is based exclusively on automated processing and has legal consequences or a considerable adverse effect, the controller must inform the data subject. On request, the person may express their view and request review by a natural person; federal bodies must designate such decisions. The Act has exceptions, including where an eligible contract-related request is granted or the person explicitly consented to automation.

applies_to.conditions: Only automated individual decisions with legal consequences or considerable adverse effects; the Art. 21(3) exceptions and federal-body hearing qualification apply.

evidence: Decision notices identifying exclusively automated consequential decisions
Procedure and records for a person's request to express a view or obtain human review

obligations.title: Assess high-risk personal-data processing before deployment
obligations.plain: Before processing likely to create a high risk to a person's personality or fundamental rights, the controller must complete a data protection impact assessment describing the processing, risks and protective measures. High risk depends on the nature, extent, circumstances and purpose, including large-scale sensitive-data processing or large-scale systematic monitoring of public areas; residual high risk generally requires prior consultation with the FDPIC, subject to statutory exceptions.

applies_to.conditions: Applies only where personal-data processing is likely to present high risk; statutory exemptions and the certified-product/code-of-conduct route are set out in Arts. 22–23.

evidence: Completed DPIA with processing description, risk evaluation and safeguards
FDPIC consultation record where residual high risk remains and consultation is required

obligations.title: Report high-risk personal-data security breaches
obligations.plain: A controller must notify the FDPIC as quickly as possible of a data-security breach likely to result in a high risk to a person's personality or fundamental rights, describing the breach, its consequences and measures taken or planned. A processor must notify the controller as quickly as possible; the controller must inform affected people where needed for their protection or at the FDPIC's request.

applies_to.conditions: Only where AI-related personal data are involved and a breach is likely to create a high risk to data subjects.

evidence: Data-breach response runbook and assessment of high-risk notification thresholds
FDPIC notice, affected-person notice, and incident documentation where required

obligations.title: Provide access information, including about automated decisions
obligations.plain: On request, a person may ask whether personal data about them is being processed and receive information needed to exercise their rights. This includes the purpose, available source of data not collected from them, and, if applicable, whether an automated individual decision was taken and the logic behind it, subject to the Act's exceptions.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to personal data within the FADP's scope; access rights may be limited in the cases set out in Arts. 26–27.

evidence: Access-request process and response template for AI-related processing
Information supplied about data sources and automated-decision logic when applicable

obligations.title: Log qualifying automated processing and keep logs protected
obligations.plain: Private controllers and processors must log specified data operations and access when they automate large-volume sensitive-data processing or high-risk profiling and preventive measures cannot ensure protection. Federal bodies and their processors must log specified operations for sensitive data, profiling and covered law-enforcement processing; for other automated processing they must assess fundamental-rights risks and decide whether and how far to log. Required logs identify who did what and when, are kept at least one year, and are separated and access-restricted.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to automated processing of personal data; private-sector logging depends on the Art. 4(1) risk conditions, while federal-body duties are specified in Art. 4(2).

evidence: Written risk assessment and decision on logging for covered automated processing
Protected logs with access restrictions and at least one-year retention where Art. 4 requires them

obligations.title: Federal bodies: assess logging needs for legacy automated processing by the transition deadline
obligations.plain: Federal bodies and their processors must assess in writing, by 31 December 2026, whether automated personal-data processing planned or started before 1 December 2025 needs logging (the Art. 4(2) assessment); if logging is needed, it must be implemented by 31 December 2029. This transition does not cover automated processing of sensitive personal data, profiling, or processing within the law-enforcement data-protection directive, which must be logged without it. Private controllers are not covered; their logging duty is in Art. 4(1).

applies_to.conditions: Federal bodies and their processors only (Art. 4(2) and 2bis). Only legacy automated processing begun or planned before the 29 October 2025 amendment came into force on 1 December 2025; excluded categories remain subject to Art. 4(2) without this transition.

evidence: Written Art. 4(2) assessment by 31 December 2026
Logging controls implemented by 31 December 2029 where the assessment finds they are needed
obligations.notes: Art. 46(1) sets two separate deadlines; the second applies only if the logging assessment finds logging necessary. It refers to the Art. 4(2) assessment, which binds federal bodies and their processors, so it does not apply to private controllers (corrected 5 November 2026; earlier versions tagged all roles).

obligations.title: Use OFCOM's voluntary AI Code of Conduct toolkit if adopting self-regulation
obligations.plain: OFCOM's toolkit helps associations and businesses create voluntary AI guidelines, with suggested texts on 10 topics and a process for developing and improving commitments. It is not legislation and creates no mandatory duty to adopt a code.
evidence: Voluntary AI policy or code and records of periodic review, if adopted
obligations.notes: OFCOM reported the guide on 28 October 2026; it is a toolkit for voluntary commitments, not a substitute for binding FADP duties.

obligations.title: Disclose recommendation and give users a real choice
obligations.plain: Algorithmic recommendation providers must clearly tell users that recommendations are being used and disclose the service's basic principles, purpose and main operating mechanisms. They must offer a non-personalised option or an easy way to turn recommendations off, immediately stop the related service when a user opts out, and let users select or delete recommendation-related personal tags.

applies_to.conditions: Internet information services using algorithmic recommendation technology in China.

evidence: User-facing recommendation notice and current description of the recommendation service
Tested preference-off and user-tag selection/deletion flows
obligations.penalty: For the specified breaches, after warning and correction orders, refusal to correct or a serious case can lead to suspension of information updates and a CNY 10,000–100,000 fine (Art. 31), unless another law provides otherwise.

obligations.title: File public-opinion or mobilisation-capable recommendation services
obligations.plain: Providers whose recommendation services have public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capability must file service and algorithm details, including a self-assessment report, within 10 working days of launch; changes are due within 10 working days and cancellation within 20 working days after termination. They must complete the required security assessment and display the filing number and public filing link after filing.

applies_to.conditions: Only algorithmic recommendation services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capability.

evidence: Filing receipt and filed self-assessment, with a change/cancellation calendar
Security-assessment record and public-facing filing number/link
obligations.penalty: Failure to meet specified filing duties can lead, after warning and correction orders, to suspension of information updates and a CNY 10,000–100,000 fine; deceptive or false filings can be revoked and fined (Arts. 31, 33).

obligations.title: Verify identity for posting and label deep-synthesis output
obligations.plain: Deep-synthesis providers must authenticate users' real identities before allowing them to publish information. They must add a technical label to content generated or edited through the service; where the specified service types could confuse the public, the content also needs a prominent notice, and labels must not be deleted, altered or concealed.

applies_to.conditions: The real-name rule is a condition for information-publishing services; prominent labels apply to the listed services where public confusion or mistaken belief is possible.

evidence: Identity-verification and publishing-gate records
Samples and technical tests showing labels persist on generated or edited content
obligations.penalty: The Measures refer violations to applicable laws and administrative regulations; serious consequences can be punished more severely (Art. 22). No standalone fine is specified here.

obligations.title: Assess and file specified deep-synthesis services
obligations.plain: Providers of services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capability must complete algorithm filing, updates and cancellation under the Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions, and display the filing number. Safety assessments are required for specified face/voice and sensitive non-biometric models or templates, and before launching new products, applications or functions with public-opinion or mobilisation attributes.

applies_to.conditions: Filing applies to services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capability; model/template assessment covers the categories in Art. 15.

evidence: Filing records and public filing-number display
Assessment reports for covered models, templates and new products/functions
obligations.penalty: Violations are handled under applicable laws and administrative regulations; serious consequences attract stricter punishment (Art. 22). No standalone fine is specified here.

obligations.title: Use lawful, governed data for public-facing GenAI services
obligations.plain: Providers must use training data and foundation models from lawful sources, respect intellectual property, obtain consent or another legal basis where training involves personal information, and improve data quality. They must also set workable data-labelling rules, assess annotation quality and train and supervise annotators.

applies_to.conditions: GenAI services provided to the public in China; non-public R&D and applications are outside the Measures' stated scope.

evidence: Training-data and foundation-model provenance, rights and personal-data legal-basis records
Annotation policy, sampling-quality checks and annotator training records
obligations.penalty: Applicable laws may impose penalties; otherwise authorities may warn, criticize, order correction and suspend the service for refusal or serious cases (Art. 21). No standalone fine is specified in these Measures.

obligations.title: Control harmful outputs and provide user safeguards
obligations.plain: Providers must not generate content prohibited by law and must take effective measures against specified discrimination and rights violations, while improving transparency and accuracy/reliability in light of service type. They must state intended users, contexts and uses, protect minors from excessive dependence, promptly stop and remediate illegal content, report it where required, and maintain a usable complaints channel with a published process and response times.

applies_to.conditions: Public-facing GenAI services within the Measures' scope in China.

evidence: Content-safety and remediation records, including reports of illegal output
Published service-scope notice, minors safeguards and complaint/response log
obligations.penalty: Applicable laws may impose penalties; otherwise authorities may warn, criticize, order correction and suspend the service for refusal or serious cases (Art. 21). No standalone fine is specified in these Measures.

obligations.title: Assess and file qualifying public-facing GenAI services
obligations.plain: Providers of generative AI services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capability must conduct a security assessment under applicable rules and complete algorithm filing, including subsequent changes and cancellation, under the Algorithmic Recommendation Provisions.

applies_to.conditions: Only services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capability; the Measures apply to services offered to the public within China.

evidence: Security-assessment report or confirmation of completion
Algorithm filing receipt, change records and cancellation record if service ends
obligations.penalty: Applicable laws may impose penalties; otherwise authorities may warn, criticize, order correction and suspend the service for refusal or serious cases (Art. 21). No standalone fine is specified in these Measures.

obligations.title: Label and verify AI-generated content across the service chain
obligations.plain: In-scope service providers must add explicit labels in the specified content types and contexts, preserve them in exported files, and embed implicit metadata with content attributes, provider name or code, and content number; they must explain labelling in user agreements and follow mandatory GB 45438-2025. Content-distribution providers must check metadata and add prominent notices for marked, declared or suspected generated content, while app-distribution platforms must verify labelling materials and users must declare and label generated content when publishing it. If a user requests content without an explicit label, the provider may supply it only after an agreement establishes user duties and it retains related logs for at least six months.

applies_to.conditions: Providers covered by the Algorithmic Recommendation, Deep Synthesis or GenAI rules; distribution-platform and user duties apply when content is distributed or posted through the relevant services.

evidence: Media samples and metadata checks for required explicit/implicit labels and distribution-platform notices
User agreement and log-retention setting for unlabelled-content requests; app-store labelling-review records
obligations.penalty: Violations are handled under applicable laws, administrative regulations and departmental rules (Art. 13); the Measures do not set a standalone fine.
obligations.notes: The official national-standards catalogue lists the Chinese GB 45438-2025 as mandatory (强标), current and effective from 2025-09-01; the English listing is marked guidance.

obligations.title: Implement the mandatory AI-content labelling method
obligations.plain: GB 45438-2025 specifies technical methods for explicit labels and implicit file-metadata labels for generative-service and content-distribution providers. The official catalogue classifies the Chinese standard as compulsory (强标), current, and effective from 1 September 2025; the English version is listed as guidance.

applies_to.conditions: Standard applies to providers of generated/synthetic content services and content-distribution services conducting AI-content labelling.

evidence: Conformance test results for visible-label placement and file metadata format
Metadata examples showing required generation and dissemination fields where applicable
obligations.cite: GB 45438-2025 Clauses 4–6 and normative Annex E

obligations.title: Recognise the Cybersecurity Law's AI governance mandate
obligations.plain: Article 20 directs the state to support AI basic research and key technologies, training-data and computing infrastructure, AI ethics norms, risk monitoring and assessment, and safety supervision; it also supports use of AI to improve cybersecurity. This is a state policy and government mandate, not a standalone technical duty or AI-specific penalty for private AI providers.

applies_to.conditions: The provision is directed to the state and government policy implementation; it does not itself specify an individual-provider compliance checklist.

evidence: Public-sector AI governance, risk-monitoring or safety-supervision implementation records
obligations.notes: The State Council's 2026 Legislative Work Plan calls for accelerating comprehensive AI legislation and related rules for shared AI inputs and key use cases. As of 2026-11-04 this is a proposed work-plan priority, not enacted law; the cited plan provides no draft text or fixed enactment date.

obligations.title: Govern human-like interaction safety and training data
obligations.plain: Providers of covered anthropomorphic interactive services must not generate the prohibited content or engage in specified harmful, manipulative or dependence-inducing conduct. They must maintain lifecycle safety, ethics, content and risk-response controls, and use legally sourced, checked and diverse training data with safeguards against poisoning and leakage.

applies_to.conditions: Services offered to the public in China that simulate human personality, thinking and communication styles through continuous emotional interaction; ordinary customer support or Q&A without sustained emotional interaction is excluded.

evidence: Lifecycle risk, ethics and incident-response procedures for the interactive service
Training-data provenance, poisoning/leakage safeguards and periodic data review
obligations.penalty: Where another law does not govern, authorities may warn, criticize, order correction and suspend related activity; serious/refusal cases can lead to service suspension and CNY 10,000–100,000 (Art. 30).

obligations.title: Protect interactive data and sensitive information
obligations.plain: Providers must protect user interaction data, may not give it to third parties without a legal basis or the user's clear consent, and must provide options to copy or delete interaction history. They may not use interaction data that is sensitive personal information to train models unless another law or administrative regulation permits it or the user gives separate consent; processing personal information of children under 14 also requires guardian consent and a compliance audit.

applies_to.conditions: Covered anthropomorphic interactive services; heightened duties apply to sensitive interaction data and personal information of children under 14.

evidence: Data-sharing and model-training legal-basis/consent records, including separate consent where relied on
User copy/delete functionality and under-14 guardian-consent/audit records
obligations.penalty: Where another law does not govern, penalties under Art. 30 include service suspension and CNY 10,000–100,000 for serious/refusal cases; if harm to life or health results, CNY 100,000–200,000.

obligations.title: Protect minors and intervene in safety crises
obligations.plain: Providers must respond to serious user distress and imminent threats to life or health with appropriate intervention, and may need to contact a guardian or emergency contact. They must not offer virtual relatives or virtual partners to minors; services to under-14s otherwise require guardian consent, and providers must offer a minors mode and safeguards, while giving older users prominent risk guidance and help.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to covered anthropomorphic interactive services; under-14 and elderly-person duties are triggered when those users receive the service.

evidence: Minors-mode settings, age/guardian-consent controls and risk-notification records
Crisis escalation procedure and samples of older-user safety guidance
obligations.penalty: Where another law does not govern, Art. 30 allows service suspension and CNY 10,000–100,000 for serious/refusal cases; where life/health harm results, CNY 100,000–200,000.

obligations.title: Disclose AI identity and allow users to leave
obligations.plain: Providers must meet AI-generated-content labelling duties and clearly tell users they are interacting with an AI rather than a person. They must visibly remind users who show excessive dependence that the interaction is AI-generated, remind users after each continuous session exceeding two hours, and promptly stop when asked to exit without using continued interaction to obstruct them.

applies_to.conditions: Covered anthropomorphic interactive services; dynamic dependence warnings are triggered by signs of excessive dependence or addiction.

evidence: First-use AI disclosure and content-labeling test samples
Two-hour and dependence-warning tests, plus verified immediate exit flow
obligations.penalty: Where another law does not govern, Art. 30 allows service suspension and CNY 10,000–100,000 for serious/refusal cases; where life/health harm results, CNY 100,000–200,000.

obligations.title: Assess and file human-like interactive services
obligations.plain: Providers must submit a security-assessment report to the provincial cyberspace authority when launching a covered service or related function, making a major change through new technology, reaching 1 million registered users or 100,000 monthly active users, or facing specified safety risks; the assessment covers training data, safeguards, user demographics, crisis intervention and complaints. Providers must also complete algorithm filing and updates/cancellation, and app-distribution platforms must verify applicable assessment and filing materials before listing and in routine management.

applies_to.conditions: Assessment thresholds and triggers are in Art. 22; algorithm filing and annual verification apply to providers, while Art. 25 platform duties apply to app-distribution platforms.

evidence: Provincial security-assessment report and trigger/threshold monitoring record
Algorithm filing and annual verification record, plus app-store safety review
obligations.penalty: Where another law does not govern, failure can result in warnings, correction orders, service suspension and CNY 10,000–100,000; life/health harm with consequences can bring CNY 100,000–200,000 (Art. 30).

obligations.title: Apply the Convention to public-sector AI and address risks from other private actors
obligations.plain: Each Party must apply the Convention to AI lifecycle activities by its public authorities and private actors acting on their behalf. For other private actors, each Party must address risks and impacts consistently with the Convention's object and purpose, and declare whether it will apply the treaty principles and obligations or take other appropriate measures.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to lifecycle activities with potential to interfere with human rights, democracy or the rule of law. This is a duty of a State Party, not a directly applicable treaty duty on companies; national-defence matters and pre-deployment R&D are excluded, except testing with such potential. Other private-actor coverage follows the Party's Article 3 implementation choice.

evidence: National implementation measure specifying the Article 3 approach for private actors
Inventory of AI lifecycle activities by public authorities and contractors acting on their behalf
obligations.notes: Convention-wide application depends on entry into force; national implementation determines private-actor duties.
obligations.instrument_short: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention
obligations.cite: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention Art. 3(1)(a)–(b)

obligations.title: Protect dignity, equality, privacy, accountability and reliability in AI activities
obligations.plain: Parties must ensure AI lifecycle activities respect human dignity and individual autonomy, accountability and responsibility, equality and non-discrimination, privacy and personal-data protection, reliability, and safe innovation. The Convention requires Parties to give effect to these principles through measures consistent with the instrument and their legal systems.

applies_to.conditions: State-Party measures apply to covered public-authority activities and private actors acting on their behalf; wider private-sector implementation is determined under Art. 3(1)(b).

evidence: Policies and assessments showing how public-sector AI use addresses the Convention principles
obligations.instrument_short: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention
obligations.cite: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention Arts. 7, 9–13

obligations.title: Provide context- and risk-appropriate transparency and oversight
obligations.plain: Each Party must adopt or maintain measures ensuring adequate transparency and oversight requirements tailored to the context and risks of AI lifecycle activities. The Article expressly includes measures concerning identification of content generated by AI systems.

applies_to.conditions: Treaty obligations are on Parties; operational requirements for providers and deployers depend on applicable domestic implementation and the Article 3 scope.

evidence: Transparency and oversight rules tailored to public-sector AI contexts and risk
Measures for identifying AI-generated content where appropriate under the implementation framework
obligations.instrument_short: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention
obligations.cite: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention Art. 8

obligations.title: Ensure effective remedies and information to challenge consequential AI use
obligations.plain: To the extent required by a Party's international obligations and consistent with its domestic legal system, it must ensure accessible and effective remedies for human-rights violations arising from AI lifecycle activities. Measures include documenting relevant information, making it available to authorised bodies and, where appropriate, affected people, enabling them to contest decisions substantially informed by AI, and providing a way to complain to competent authorities.

applies_to.conditions: The Convention sets duties on Parties; the remedies obligation is expressly qualified by existing international obligations and the domestic legal system.

evidence: Documented AI system use and information-access procedure for affected people
Accessible complaint and contest process linked to competent authorities
obligations.instrument_short: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention
obligations.cite: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention Art. 14(1)–(2)

obligations.title: Provide procedural safeguards and, where appropriate, AI-interaction notice
obligations.plain: Each Party must ensure effective procedural guarantees, safeguards and rights where an AI system significantly affects the enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms, consistent with applicable international and domestic law. Parties must also seek context-appropriate notice that a person is interacting with an AI system rather than a human being.

applies_to.conditions: The interaction notice is context-dependent; the treaty's procedural-safeguard requirements apply where human rights and fundamental freedoms are significantly affected.

evidence: Procedural safeguards for people significantly affected by public-sector AI
Notice design and records for AI interactions where appropriate to context
obligations.instrument_short: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention
obligations.cite: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention Art. 15(1)–(2)

obligations.title: Manage AI risks and impacts iteratively across the lifecycle
obligations.plain: Each Party must adopt or maintain graduated, context-sensitive measures to identify, assess, prevent and mitigate AI risks to human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Measures apply iteratively, consider impact severity and probability and relevant stakeholders, monitor and document risks and impacts, and require testing where appropriate; Parties must assess whether incompatible uses warrant a moratorium, ban or other measures.

applies_to.conditions: Treaty duties are on Parties and apply to covered lifecycle activities; each Party's measures must reflect context, intended use and risk.

evidence: Iterative human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law risk and impact assessments
Documented mitigation, monitoring and testing decisions across the AI lifecycle
obligations.instrument_short: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention
obligations.cite: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention Art. 16(1)–(4)

obligations.title: Establish independent and effective oversight mechanisms
obligations.plain: Each Party must establish or designate one or more effective mechanisms to oversee compliance with the Convention. Those mechanisms must be independent and impartial and have the powers, expertise and resources needed to perform their duties effectively.

applies_to.conditions: This is an institutional duty of each Party; it does not itself create an AI-authorisation or registration requirement for companies.

evidence: Designation or establishment of an adequately resourced, independent oversight mechanism
Published oversight mandate, powers and accountability arrangements
obligations.instrument_short: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention
obligations.cite: Council of Europe AI Framework Convention Art. 26(1)–(2)

obligations.title: Do not build or use banned AI practices
obligations.plain: Placing on the market, putting into service or using AI for banned practices is prohibited. The list includes manipulative or deceptive techniques that cause significant harm, exploiting vulnerabilities, social scoring, predicting crime from profiling alone, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion recognition at work or school, biometric categorisation inferring sensitive traits, and real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement in public spaces (with narrow exceptions).
evidence: Use-case screening record against each Art. 5 practice, signed by an accountable owner
obligations.penalty: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(3))

obligations.title: Do not offer AI that creates non-consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material
obligations.plain: From 2 December 2026 it is prohibited to place on the market, put into service or use an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic intimate or sexually explicit material of an identifiable person without that person's explicit consent, or that generates child sexual abuse material.
evidence: Output filters and abuse-testing results for intimate and sexual content
Policy and enforcement log for misuse reports
obligations.penalty: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(3))
obligations.notes: Added by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI). Application date set in Art. 113(a).

obligations.title: Support AI literacy of staff who run or use AI
obligations.plain: Providers and deployers must take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff and others operating AI on their behalf, taking into account their knowledge, the context of use and the people affected. As amended in 2026, this does not require guaranteeing a specific literacy level for any individual; the Commission and Member States must support companies, especially SMEs.
evidence: Training plan and attendance records for people who operate or use AI systems
obligations.notes: Paragraphs 1 to 3 amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI.

obligations.title: Tell people they are interacting with an AI system
obligations.plain: Providers must design AI systems that interact directly with people so those people are informed they are interacting with an AI, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed person from the context.
evidence: Screenshot or transcript showing the AI disclosure at the first interaction
obligations.penalty: Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4))

obligations.title: Mark AI-generated content in a machine-readable way
obligations.plain: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they are detectable as AI-generated, using effective, interoperable, robust and reliable techniques as far as technically feasible. Assistive editing functions that do not substantially alter the input are exempt. Systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026.
evidence: Description of the marking technique (for example signed metadata plus imperceptible watermark) and detection test results
obligations.penalty: Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4))
obligations.notes: The voluntary EU Code of Practice on marking and labelling (final June 2026) describes a layered approach (metadata and watermarking) as a way to show compliance.
obligations.cite: EU AI Act Art. 50(2) and Art. 111(4)

obligations.title: Inform people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation
obligations.plain: Deployers of an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system must inform the people exposed to it and process personal data in line with the GDPR and related EU data protection law.
evidence: Notice text shown to exposed persons and the GDPR legal basis record
obligations.notes: Emotion recognition at work or in education is banned outright by Art. 5(1)(f), with medical and safety exceptions.

obligations.title: Label deepfakes and AI-written public-interest text
obligations.plain: Deployers who generate or manipulate image, audio or video that is a deepfake must disclose that it is artificially generated or manipulated (a lighter duty applies to evidently artistic, satirical or fictional works). Deployers publishing AI-generated text to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose it, unless it underwent human review or editorial control and someone holds editorial responsibility.
evidence: Examples of published labels and the editorial review procedure for public-interest text
obligations.penalty: Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4))

obligations.title: Document general-purpose AI models, respect copyright and publish a training-data summary
obligations.plain: Providers of general-purpose AI models must keep technical documentation for authorities, give integrators the information they need, put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law (including text-and-data-mining opt-outs) and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content using the AI Office template. Open-source models are exempt from some documentation duties unless they pose systemic risk.
evidence: Model documentation, downstream information pack, copyright policy and public training-content summary
obligations.penalty: Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 101), enforceable from 2 Aug 2026
obligations.notes: Models placed on the market before 2 Aug 2025 have until 2 Aug 2027 (Art. 111(3)). The GPAI Code of Practice (July 2025) is a voluntary way to show compliance.

obligations.title: Evaluate and secure general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
obligations.plain: Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must evaluate models with state-of-the-art protocols including adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and ensure adequate cybersecurity.

applies_to.conditions: Models classified as having systemic risk (presumed above 10^25 FLOP of training compute, Art. 51)

evidence: Evaluation and red-team reports, systemic-risk assessment, incident log and security measures

obligations.title: Check whether your system is high-risk
obligations.plain: A system is high-risk if it is a safety component of (or is) a product under Annex I law that needs third-party conformity assessment, or if it falls into an Annex III area such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services and credit, law enforcement, migration, or justice and democratic processes. Some Annex III systems are not high-risk if they only perform narrow or preparatory tasks and do not profile people (Art. 6(3)); that assessment must be documented.
evidence: Documented classification decision, including any Art. 6(3) exemption reasoning
obligations.notes: Annex III systems from 2 Dec 2027; Annex I product systems from 2 Aug 2028 (Art. 113(c) as amended).
obligations.cite: EU AI Act Art. 6 and Annex III

obligations.title: Meet the high-risk requirements (risk, data, documentation, logs, transparency, oversight, robustness)
obligations.plain: Providers of high-risk systems must run a risk management system across the life cycle (Art. 9), govern training, validation and test data (Art. 10), keep technical documentation per Annex IV (Art. 11), enable automatic event logging (Art. 12), give deployers clear instructions (Art. 13), design for effective human oversight including the ability to stop the system (Art. 14), and achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Art. 15).

applies_to.conditions: Only for systems classified as high-risk under Art. 6

evidence: Risk register, data sheets, Annex IV file, logging design, instructions for use, oversight design and test results
obligations.penalty: Up to EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4))
obligations.notes: Annex III systems from 2 Dec 2027; Annex I product systems from 2 Aug 2028.

obligations.title: Run a quality management system and complete conformity assessment
obligations.plain: Providers of high-risk systems must have a documented quality management system, complete the applicable conformity assessment before placing the system on the market, draw up an EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking.

applies_to.conditions: Only for systems classified as high-risk under Art. 6. Simplified QMS options for SMEs and small mid-caps.

evidence: QMS manual, conformity assessment record, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking

obligations.title: Register high-risk systems in the EU database
obligations.plain: Before placing a high-risk Annex III system on the market, providers must register themselves and the system in the EU database. Public authorities and bodies acting on their behalf must register their use of high-risk systems. Law-enforcement and migration systems go into a secure non-public section.
evidence: EU database registration reference
obligations.notes: The Digital Omnibus simplified registration for Annex III systems that are exempted from high-risk status under Art. 6(3).

obligations.title: Monitor after release and report serious incidents
obligations.plain: Providers of high-risk systems must run post-market monitoring and report serious incidents to market surveillance authorities immediately after establishing a likely causal link, and no later than 15 days after becoming aware; no later than 2 days for widespread infringements or serious disruption of critical infrastructure; no later than 10 days in case of death.
evidence: Post-market monitoring plan and incident reporting runbook with the 15, 10 and 2 day clocks

obligations.title: Appoint an EU authorised representative if you are outside the EU
obligations.plain: Providers of high-risk AI systems and of general-purpose AI models established outside the EU must appoint an authorised representative in the EU by written mandate before placing their system or model on the EU market.

applies_to.conditions: Provider established outside the EU

evidence: Signed mandate with the authorised representative
obligations.notes: Applicable for GPAI providers (Art. 54) since 2 Aug 2025; for high-risk providers (Art. 22) from 2 Dec 2027 or 2 Aug 2028.

obligations.title: Use high-risk systems as instructed, with competent human oversight and logs
obligations.plain: Deployers of high-risk systems must use them according to the instructions, assign human oversight to competent people, monitor operation, keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, inform workers and their representatives before workplace use, and inform people subject to decisions made or assisted by the system.
evidence: Named oversight owners, log retention setting of six months or more, worker notice, notice to affected persons

obligations.title: Do a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use
obligations.plain: Before first use of certain high-risk systems, deployers that are public bodies or private entities providing public services, and deployers of credit-scoring or life and health insurance pricing systems, must assess the impact on fundamental rights and notify the market surveillance authority of the results.
evidence: Completed FRIA using the AI Office template and the notification receipt

obligations.title: Explain high-risk decisions on request
obligations.plain: People affected by a decision based on output of an Annex III high-risk system that produces legal or similarly significant effects can obtain a clear and meaningful explanation from the deployer of the role of the AI system and the main elements of the decision.
evidence: Explanation request procedure and response template
obligations.notes: Application date follows the high-risk timeline; confirm in the consolidated text.

obligations.title: Restrict significant automated decisions using special-category data
obligations.plain: A significant decision with legal or similarly significant effects that is based solely on automated processing and uses special-category data is barred unless the decision relies entirely on explicit consent, or is necessary for a contract or required/authorised by law and the substantial-public-interest condition in Article 9(2)(g) applies. A significant decision relying in whole or part on the recognised legitimate-interests basis in Article 6(1)(ea) also cannot be made solely by automated processing.

applies_to.conditions: Controllers making a significant decision based solely on automated processing of personal data; Article 22A defines the decision and meaningful-human-involvement threshold.

evidence: Decision inventory showing which significant decisions are solely automated and whether profiling is used
Lawful-basis, Article 9 condition, and exception analysis for each covered decision
obligations.notes: This is not the former general prohibition with three exceptions. Article 22B sets specific restrictions, including on special-category data and Article 6(1)(ea).

obligations.title: Give people safeguards for significant automated decisions
obligations.plain: For a significant decision based at least partly on personal data and solely on automated processing, the controller must provide safeguards that give the person information about the decision, let them make representations, obtain human intervention by the controller, and contest the decision.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to controllers making significant decisions solely by automated processing, including profiling; Article 22D allows regulations to supplement or specify safeguards.

evidence: Information notice describing the decision and a record of when it is provided
Working representation, human-intervention and contest processes, with records of requests and outcomes

obligations.title: Safeguard automated law-enforcement decisions
obligations.plain: Controllers processing personal data for law-enforcement purposes may not make a significant decision based solely on automated processing that uses sensitive processing, except with explicit consent or where required or authorised by law. Significant solely automated decisions must generally include information, an opportunity for representations, human intervention and a means to contest, subject to the statutory exceptions and reconsideration safeguards.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to controllers processing under Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 for law-enforcement purposes; the decision must have an adverse legal or similarly significant effect.

evidence: Record showing the Part 3 law-enforcement purpose, decision threshold and sensitive-processing condition
Safeguard and human-reconsideration procedure, including exceptions relied upon

obligations.title: Assess and reduce illegal-content risks on in-scope services
obligations.plain: Providers of regulated user-to-user and search services must assess illegal-content risks, keep assessments up to date (including before significant service changes), and take proportionate measures to prevent priority illegal content and mitigate identified harms and offence-facilitation risks. AI content shared by users or encountered through search can be in scope like other content.

applies_to.conditions: Only services meeting the Act's user-to-user or search definitions and UK-link rules. A one-to-one chatbot that neither enables user sharing nor searches multiple sites is generally outside Part 3; see Ofcom's chatbot guidance.

evidence: Service-specific illegal-content risk assessment that covers chatbot, generative features and significant changes
Content moderation, reporting and complaints controls with review records
obligations.penalty: Ofcom may impose a penalty up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is greater.
obligations.notes: Ofcom's 2025/2026 guidance explains that user-shared AI outputs are user-generated content. The Crime and Policing Act 2026 added OSA s.216A, an enabling power to extend duties by regulations; that power itself does not create a new direct provider duty.

obligations.title: Assess and mitigate risks to children
obligations.plain: Providers of regulated user-to-user and search services likely to be accessed by children must assess risks to children and take proportionate steps to mitigate and manage them. User-to-user services must prevent children encountering primary-priority harmful content using age verification or estimation where required, and protect children from other harmful content.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to in-scope services likely to be accessed by children; duties vary by service type, identified risk, content and child age group. AI-generated content shared between users is assessed as other user-generated content.

evidence: Children’s access/risk assessment covering AI chatbot and generated-content features
Age-assurance and child-safety measures, with evidence of effectiveness and periodic review
obligations.penalty: Ofcom may impose a penalty up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is greater.

obligations.title: Age-gate provider-published pornography
obligations.plain: A service with regulated provider-published pornographic content and UK links must use highly effective age verification or estimation so children are not normally able to encounter it. The provider must keep a written record of its method and privacy considerations and publish a summary; provider-published content may include material produced through an automated tool.

applies_to.conditions: Part 5 covers provider-published pornography, including where the provider uses an automated tool; user-generated pornography is excluded from Part 5 and may instead trigger Part 3 duties.

evidence: Highly effective age-assurance design and test results
Written record and public summary of age-assurance methods and privacy considerations
obligations.penalty: Ofcom may impose a penalty up to £18 million or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is greater.
obligations.notes: Ofcom's chatbot guidance says the Act covers chatbots meeting user-to-user/search definitions and services publishing pornography, but not every standalone chatbot.

obligations.title: Do not create or request non-consensual purported intimate images
obligations.plain: In England and Wales, a person commits an offence by intentionally creating a purported intimate image of an adult without consent and without a reasonable belief in consent, or by intentionally requesting its creation on the same basis. The offence covers qualifying synthetic images; the Act defines the image and provides a reasonable-excuse defence.

applies_to.conditions: The offences apply to adults and extend to England and Wales only; the Act's section 138 offences do not extend to Scotland. A narrow statutory exception applies to certain edits of an existing image.

evidence: Product and use-case controls against creating or requesting non-consensual intimate imagery
Records of abuse reports and actions taken to prevent or respond to prohibited use
obligations.notes: Section 141(5)(c) limits the new offences to England and Wales. Scotland had consulted on possible equivalent offences in 2026; this file does not treat that proposal as law.
obligations.cite: Non-consensual purported intimate images DUAA 2025 s. 138 (SOA 2003 ss. 66E–66F)

obligations.title: Do not make or supply purported intimate-image generators
obligations.plain: It is an offence to make or adapt, or supply or offer to supply, a thing for use as a generator of purported intimate images. “Thing” includes a program, electronic information or a service; a defence is available for taking all reasonable steps to prevent non-consensual use.

applies_to.conditions: The substantive offence applies in England and Wales. Section 99(5) separately extends the extraterritorial application rule to UK-incorporated bodies and associations; ordinary internet-service-provider safe harbours also apply.

evidence: Design-purpose review and access controls for image-generation features
Documented safeguards and abuse-testing showing reasonable steps to prevent non-consensual use
obligations.notes: Scotland's adult creation offence was not enacted by the cutoff; the Scottish Government consulted on possible offences in 2026. Section 99's general offence is E&W; subsection (5) concerns extraterritorial application for UK bodies.
obligations.cite: Intimate-image and child-abuse-image generator offences CPA 2026 s. 99 (SOA 2003 s. 66I)

obligations.article: CPA 2026 ss. 72 and 74 (SOA 2003 s. 46A; Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982 s. 52D)
obligations.title: Do not make, possess or supply child sexual-abuse image generators
obligations.plain: The enacted provisions create offences involving making or adapting, possessing, supplying or offering to supply a thing made for creating or facilitating child sexual-abuse images. “Thing” includes a program, electronic information or a service. The England-and-Wales and Scotland provisions had not been commenced by 4 November 2026.

applies_to.conditions: Section 72 is for England and Wales; section 74 is the separate Scottish provision. Both are enacted but remain prospective pending commencement regulations.

evidence: Prohibited-use controls and testing for child sexual-abuse image generation
Records of measures to prevent creation, possession or supply of generator tools for this use
obligations.notes: Do not treat these provisions as operative duties before their commencement. Existing child-abuse-image offences may independently apply to synthetic material.
obligations.cite: Intimate-image and child-abuse-image generator offences CPA 2026 ss. 72 and 74 (SOA 2003 s. 46A; Civic Government (Scotland) Act 1982 s. 52D)

obligations.article: ATRS mandatory scope and exemptions policy
obligations.title: Publish transparency records for in-scope central-government tools
obligations.plain: Central-government departments and specified arm’s-length bodies must publish an ATRS record for algorithmic tools in beta/pilot or production that significantly influence public-effect decisions or directly interact with the public. The policy is broader than AI and is not a statute; other public-sector bodies are encouraged, not required, to use ATRS.

applies_to.conditions: Mandatory only for ministerial and non-ministerial departments and ALBs providing public/frontline services or routinely interacting with the public; sensitive information may be withheld under the policy.

evidence: Published ATRS record for every in-scope algorithmic tool, including a public-facing chatbot
Scope assessment and documented reasons for any exemption or redaction
obligations.notes: This is a mandatory cross-government policy for its defined central-government scope, not an enacted statutory duty or a general requirement for all public bodies.
obligations.cite: ATRS mandatory scope and exemptions policy

obligations.article: AI Cyber Security Code of Practice, Principles 1–13
obligations.title: Use the voluntary AI cyber-security baseline
obligations.plain: The government code recommends lifecycle cyber-security measures for AI developers and operators, including secure design and supply chains, risk assessment, access controls, documentation, testing, incident response, updates and end-of-life practices. It is voluntary and is not a statutory duty.
evidence: AI security threat and risk assessment, access-control and supply-chain records
Testing, patching, incident-response and end-of-life plans
obligations.notes: The voluntary code was published by DSIT with NCSC collaboration. The UK AI Safety Institute was renamed the AI Security Institute on 14 February 2025; it is a research institute, not a regulator or a separate binding code.
obligations.instrument_short: AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
obligations.cite: AI Cyber Security Code of Practice, Principles 1–13

obligations.title: Use the voluntary India AI governance principles and practices
obligations.plain: The Guidelines set out seven principles, recommendations across six governance pillars, an action plan and proposed institutional coordination and technical-support arrangements. They recommend that AI developers and deployers comply with existing Indian laws and voluntarily adopt measures such as risk mitigation, transparency, grievance redressal and responsible-AI practices; they do not create binding duties or a new horizontal AI law.

applies_to.conditions: Guidance for people and organisations developing or deploying AI in India; the recommendations are voluntary.

evidence: Internal responsible-AI policy mapping voluntary principles to owners and product processes
Risk or transparency report and an accessible AI-harm grievance channel
obligations.notes: The official Guidelines describe voluntary measures as optional and lacking legal enforceability or punitive action; sectoral statutes and rules remain binding independently.

obligations.title: Prevent unlawful synthetic media and label other synthetic information
obligations.plain: Intermediaries offering a computer resource that can enable creation or dissemination of synthetically generated information (SGI) must use reasonable and appropriate technical measures to prevent SGI that violates applicable law. Other SGI must carry a prominent visible label, or a prefixed disclosure for audio, and, to the extent technically feasible, permanent metadata or another provenance mechanism including a unique identifier; intermediaries must not enable removal or suppression of those labels or markers.

applies_to.conditions: Only intermediaries whose computer resources may enable, permit or facilitate creation, generation, modification, alteration, publication, transmission, sharing or dissemination of SGI.

evidence: Technical controls and test results for blocking unlawful SGI and applying visible or audio labels
Provenance/identifier implementation record and tests showing labels and metadata cannot be removed through the service
obligations.notes: Rule 2(1)(wa) limits SGI to audio, visual or audio-visual information that appears real or authentic and depicts a person or event in a way likely to be perceived as indistinguishable from a natural person or real-world event. It excludes specified routine good-faith editing, document preparation and accessibility operations. Rule 3(1)(cb) separately requires expeditious and appropriate action when the intermediary becomes aware of covered contravening SGI.
obligations.cite: IT Intermediary Rules Rule 3(3)(a)(i)–(ii) and Rule 3(3)(b)

obligations.title: Verify synthetic-media declarations before SSMI publication
obligations.plain: Before permitting information to be displayed, uploaded or published, a significant social media intermediary (SSMI) must require users to declare whether it is SGI and deploy appropriate technical measures, including automated tools, to verify the declaration in light of the content’s nature, format and source. If a declaration or verification confirms SGI, the intermediary must clearly and prominently label it; knowingly permitting, promoting or failing to act on SGI in contravention of the Rules is deemed a failure of due diligence.

applies_to.conditions: Only SSMIs as defined by Rule 2(1)(v) that enable display, upload or publication of information on their computer resources.

evidence: Pre-publication user-declaration flow and technical verification test records
Examples of prominently labelled confirmed SGI and audit trail of moderation decisions

obligations.title: Act on specified unlawful-content orders within three hours
obligations.plain: When an intermediary receives actual knowledge of unlawful information through an order of a competent court or a written, reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer or agency, it must remove or disable access to the specified information within three hours.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to covered unlawful information hosted, displayed, published, transmitted or stored on the intermediary’s computer resource; actual knowledge must arise by the channels specified in the Rule.

evidence: Intake and escalation procedure recording receipt time, legal authority, decision and completion time
Takedown log showing action within the three-hour deadline

obligations.title: Remove specified intimate or impersonating content within two hours of complaint
obligations.plain: On a complaint by an individual, or someone acting on the individual’s behalf, about content prima facie exposing private areas, showing nudity or sexual conduct, or impersonating the individual electronically (including artificially morphed images), an intermediary must take reasonable and practicable measures to remove or disable access within two hours.

applies_to.conditions: Includes content hosted, stored, published or transmitted by the intermediary; the complaint must concern one of the categories enumerated in Rule 3(2)(b).

evidence: Complaint intake timestamps and two-hour removal/disablement records
Procedure for preserving relevant evidence after action

obligations.title: Resolve intermediary grievances within seven days
obligations.plain: Intermediaries must acknowledge a grievance within 24 hours and resolve it within seven days of receipt. Specified requests to remove information or links under Rule 3(1)(b), subject to the listed exceptions, must be handled as expeditiously as possible and resolved within 36 hours.

applies_to.conditions: Grievances concern violations of the Rules or other matters pertaining to the intermediary’s computer resources.

evidence: Grievance workflow timestamps for acknowledgement, resolution and any 36-hour category
Complaint-resolution records and escalation procedures

obligations.title: Use a lawful basis and give notice before requesting consent
obligations.plain: Personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose on consent or a permitted legitimate-use basis. Before seeking consent, the Data Fiduciary must give notice describing the personal data and purpose and how the person may exercise rights and complain; consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, limited to data necessary for the specified purpose, and given by clear affirmative action.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to Data Fiduciaries processing digital personal data in India, including data collected digitally or later digitised, and certain processing outside India connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India; statutory exclusions and permitted legitimate uses apply.

evidence: Data inventory and documented lawful-purpose/consent analysis for AI processing
Versioned privacy notices and consent/withdrawal records
obligations.notes: Sections 3–6 are among the Act provisions scheduled to commence after eighteen months under G.S.R. 843(E), not on enactment in 2023.

obligations.title: Govern processors, safeguard personal data and notify breaches
obligations.plain: A Data Fiduciary remains responsible for its own processing and processing on its behalf, may engage a Data Processor only under a valid contract, and must implement technical and organisational measures, protect personal data with reasonable security safeguards and notify the Board and affected people of breaches. Rules 6 and 7 specify safeguards such as access controls, logs, backups and processor-contract terms, prompt notice to affected people, and an initial Board intimation without delay followed by detailed information within 72 hours unless the Board allows longer.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to Data Fiduciaries processing digital personal data within the Act’s territorial scope.

evidence: Data-processor contracts, security-control records, access logs and backup/retention settings
Breach response runbook and records of notices to the Board and affected Data Principals
obligations.notes: Rules 6 and 7 operationalise the safeguards and breach-intimation requirements; the official Rules text is listed in sources. The Rules’ 18-month phase-in is confirmed in Rule 1(4).
obligations.cite: DPDP Act Section 8(1)–(7); DPDP Rules 6 and 7

obligations.title: Significant Data Fiduciaries must assess and audit data and algorithms
obligations.plain: A notified Significant Data Fiduciary must appoint an India-based Data Protection Officer and an independent data auditor; Rule 13 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment and audit at least every 12 months, with significant observations reported to the Board. It must also use due diligence to verify that its technical measures, including algorithmic software used for the listed personal-data operations, are not likely to risk Data Principals’ rights; any localisation condition applies only to personal data specified by the Central Government.

applies_to.conditions: Only a Data Fiduciary or class of Data Fiduciaries formally notified as significant under section 10 and processing digital personal data.

evidence: Notification status, India-based DPO and independent-auditor appointment records
Annual DPIA/audit reports and algorithmic due-diligence assessment submitted or available to the Board
obligations.penalty: Up to INR 150 crore for breach of additional Significant Data Fiduciary obligations (section 33 and Schedule).
obligations.notes: Section 10 and Rule 13 are in the 18-month phase beginning 2027-05-13. The Act’s section 10 provides the DPO, auditor and periodic-DPIA framework; Rule 13 prescribes annual cadence and algorithmic due diligence.

obligations.title: Cooperate with national and local AI measures
obligations.plain: Utilization business operators must cooperate with measures taken by the national and local governments under Articles 4 and 5. They need only endeavor to use AI actively to improve business efficiency and advancement and create new industries.

applies_to.conditions: People developing or providing AI-enabled products or services, or using AI in business activities.

evidence: Records of cooperation with applicable national or local government AI measures
Internal record identifying the entity's AI business activities
obligations.notes: The Act has no penalties chapter. Article 16 allows government research, guidance, advice, information provision and other measures; Article 7 does not set a detailed AI risk-management checklist.

obligations.title: Follow Japan's current government AI strategy
obligations.plain: The Cabinet's second plan sets government policy across AI adoption, development capabilities, AI governance and an AI-powered society, with implementation and follow-up arrangements. It is a government strategy, not a direct compliance duty for private AI operators.

applies_to.conditions: Government policy commitment under Article 18 of the AI Promotion Act; no direct private-sector obligation.

evidence: Public implementation and follow-up materials for the plan
obligations.notes: The English text is a provisional translation; the Cabinet Office index confirms the 14 July 2026 Cabinet decision.

obligations.title: Keep AI human-centric
obligations.plain: The voluntary guidelines recommend respecting human dignity and autonomy when developing, providing or using AI, and taking steps against manipulation and automation bias. They also call for user support appropriate to the system and context.

applies_to.conditions: Nonbinding soft-law recommendations for AI business actors, including public institutions.

evidence: Human-impact review and human intervention procedures for relevant AI use cases
obligations.notes: Official English PDF is a provisional translation; refer to the Japanese text for accuracy.
obligations.cite: AI Guidelines for Business Ver1.2 Part 2.C.1

obligations.title: Assess and manage AI safety risks
obligations.plain: The guidelines recommend checking reliability, robustness and controllability, analyzing risks, and taking proportionate measures throughout development, provision and use. They also recommend defining responses for cases where AI safety is endangered.

applies_to.conditions: Voluntary, risk-based guidance for AI business actors, including public institutions.

evidence: Risk analysis, safety testing and response procedures proportionate to the use case
obligations.notes: Official English PDF is a provisional translation; refer to the Japanese text for accuracy.
obligations.cite: AI Guidelines for Business Ver1.2 Part 2.C.2

obligations.title: Protect privacy throughout the AI lifecycle
obligations.plain: The guidelines recommend observing applicable privacy laws and adopting privacy measures based on the use context and people's reasonable expectations. They also recommend a privacy policy and privacy-by-design measures appropriate to the AI system.

applies_to.conditions: Voluntary guidance; applicable personal-information laws remain binding independently.

evidence: Privacy policy and records of privacy-by-design review
obligations.notes: Official English PDF is a provisional translation; refer to the Japanese text for accuracy.
obligations.cite: AI Guidelines for Business Ver1.2 Part 2.C.4

obligations.title: Secure AI systems and services
obligations.plain: The guidelines recommend reasonable security measures suited to the technology and its lifecycle, including attention to system connections, vulnerabilities and current attack methods. The guidance does not replace binding cybersecurity or sectoral rules.

applies_to.conditions: Voluntary guidance for AI business actors, including public institutions.

evidence: Security testing and documented remediation of relevant AI system vulnerabilities
obligations.notes: Official English PDF is a provisional translation; refer to the Japanese text for accuracy.
obligations.cite: AI Guidelines for Business Ver1.2 Part 2.C.5

obligations.title: Provide proportionate information about AI
obligations.plain: The guidelines recommend making AI systems verifiable and providing stakeholders with information about AI use, capabilities, limitations, risks and appropriate use, to a reasonable extent that is technically possible. They also recommend keeping relevant process and decision logs where possible.

applies_to.conditions: Voluntary recommendations; disclosure should reflect the social context and system purpose.

evidence: Stakeholder-facing system information and relevant decision or operation logs
obligations.notes: Official English PDF is a provisional translation; refer to the Japanese text for accuracy.
obligations.cite: AI Guidelines for Business Ver1.2 Part 2.C.6

obligations.title: Document AI accountability
obligations.plain: The guidelines recommend traceability of data and decisions, assigning a responsible person, clarifying shared responsibilities, explaining conformity to the common principles and documenting relevant information. The scope of these steps should reflect the actor's role and the system's risks.

applies_to.conditions: Voluntary accountability recommendations for AI business actors, including public institutions.

evidence: Named accountability owner, responsibility allocation and governance records
obligations.notes: Official English PDF is a provisional translation; refer to the Japanese text for accuracy.
obligations.cite: AI Guidelines for Business Ver1.2 Part 2.C.7

obligations.title: Tell users in advance when a service uses generative or high-impact AI
obligations.plain: An AI business operator providing a product or service using generative or high-impact AI must notify users in advance that the product or service is operated using that AI. The Decree permits several notice methods and provides exceptions, including where AI use is evident, use is solely for the operator's internal business, or the Minister designates an exception.

applies_to.conditions: Products or services using generative AI or high-impact AI; the Decree's exceptions apply.

evidence: User-facing notice text, screenshots, or service-flow recording showing advance notice
Documented exception analysis where the operator relies on a Decree exception
obligations.penalty: Up to KRW 30 million administrative fine under Article 43(1)(1); MSIT announced that penalties are deferred during an enforcement grace period of at least one year, subject to highly exceptional cases.
obligations.notes: The Act applies to conduct outside Korea that affects the Korean market or users (Art. 4(1)). The English text is an official aid to understanding, not legally authoritative; current Korean consolidated text is at the instrument official_url.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 31(1); Enforcement Decree Art. 23(1), (4)

obligations.title: Identify outputs generated by generative AI
obligations.plain: An AI business operator providing generative AI or a product or service using it must indicate that the output was generated by generative AI. The Decree permits human-perceptible or machine-readable indications; a machine-readable indication must be accompanied at least once by text, voice, or another means telling users that the content was AI-generated.

applies_to.conditions: Covers generative-AI outputs; Decree exceptions may apply, including evident AI use and solely internal business use.

evidence: Output examples and a record of the visible or machine-readable indication method
Detection or user-interface test showing the indication can be perceived as required
obligations.penalty: No standalone administrative fine is specified for Article 31(2); MSIT may investigate and order correction, and failure to comply with a corrective order can incur up to KRW 30 million under Article 43(1)(3). MSIT announced a minimum one-year enforcement grace.
obligations.notes: A machine-readable marker alone is not enough under Decree Art. 23(2); users must also be told at least once by text, voice, or a similar means. The English translation's rendering of the compute exponent is imperfect, but this output-marking clause is legible in the official text.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 31(2); Enforcement Decree Art. 23(2), (4)

obligations.title: Clearly label realistic synthetic audio, images, and video
obligations.plain: If an operator provides AI-generated virtual sound, images, or video that are difficult to distinguish from real content, it must notify or label users so they can clearly recognize that the content was generated by AI. For artistic or creative work, the label may be presented in a way that does not hinder its exhibition or enjoyment; the Decree requires recognition by visual, auditory, or software means and consideration of the primary users' age and circumstances.

applies_to.conditions: AI-generated virtual sound, images, or video difficult to distinguish from real content; Decree exceptions may apply.

evidence: Examples of user-facing labels or notices on realistic synthetic media
Test record showing users can recognize the label through the relevant mode
obligations.penalty: No standalone administrative fine is specified for Article 31(3); investigation and corrective-order powers apply, with up to KRW 30 million for failure to comply with an order. MSIT announced a minimum one-year enforcement grace.
