obligations.notes: The artistic/creative-work language allows a presentation that does not hinder exhibition or enjoyment; it does not remove the requirement to disclose or label.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 31(3); Enforcement Decree Art. 23(3), (4)

obligations.title: Manage lifecycle safety risks for qualifying advanced AI systems
obligations.plain: For an AI system meeting the Decree's cumulative training-compute threshold, the operator must identify, assess, and mitigate risks throughout the lifecycle, maintain a risk-management system to monitor and respond to AI safety incidents, and submit implementation results to MSIT. The Decree requires all criteria together: at least 10^26 floating-point operations for training, use of the most advanced AI technology then in use, and a likelihood of widespread and significant effects on life, physical safety, or fundamental rights.

applies_to.conditions: All three Decree Art. 24 criteria must be met; the compute threshold alone does not trigger the duties.

evidence: Training-compute calculation and written assessment of the other two Decree criteria
Lifecycle risk and incident-management records, plus submitted results to MSIT
obligations.penalty: No standalone administrative fine is specified for Article 32; MSIT may investigate and order correction, and failure to comply with a corrective order can incur up to KRW 30 million under Article 43(1)(3). MSIT announced a minimum one-year enforcement grace.
obligations.notes: The compute number is stated as 10^26 FLOPs in MSIT's official English description of Decree Art. 24. The official English Decree rendering has an exponent/OCR issue; use the current Korean Decree and MSIT's description, and do not treat compute alone as sufficient.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 32(1)-(3); Enforcement Decree Art. 24

obligations.title: Review whether a system is high-impact AI before providing it
obligations.plain: When providing AI or a product or service using it, an AI business operator must review in advance whether the system qualifies as high-impact AI. If classification is uncertain, the operator may request confirmation from the Minister of Science and ICT; the Decree specifies the request materials and a response period of 30 days, extendable once by up to 30 days.

applies_to.conditions: Applies where AI is provided, including systems used in statutory areas that may significantly affect or pose risk to life, physical safety, or fundamental rights.

evidence: Dated high-impact classification review, including the statutory domain and risk reasoning
Confirmation request and MSIT response, if the operator sought a determination
obligations.notes: The Act's high-impact domains include energy, drinking water, health and medical services and devices, nuclear safety, criminal investigation or arrest biometrics, consequential hiring or loan judgments, transport, public-sector decisions, education, and any further domain prescribed by decree. The digital-medical-device portion took effect on 2026-01-24.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 33(1)-(4); Enforcement Decree Art. 25

obligations.title: Apply safety and trust measures to high-impact AI
obligations.plain: An operator providing high-impact AI, or a product or service using it, must implement measures under the Decree that include a risk-management plan; technically feasible explanations of final outputs, main criteria, and an overview of training data; user-protection measures; human management and oversight; and records verifying the measures. Equivalent measures under other laws may be deemed to satisfy the duty as prescribed by the Decree.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to high-impact AI or products or services using it; classification depends on statutory domains and risk criteria.

evidence: Current risk, explanation, user-protection, and human-oversight plans
Records showing measures taken and any equivalent-measures basis relied upon
obligations.penalty: No standalone administrative fine is specified for Article 34(1); MSIT may investigate and order correction, and failure to comply with a corrective order can incur up to KRW 30 million under Article 43(1)(3). MSIT announced a minimum one-year enforcement grace.
obligations.notes: Explanations are required to the extent technically feasible. The statute delegates specific measures to the Enforcement Decree and MSIT notices/guidelines.

obligations.title: Publish key high-impact AI safeguards and retain evidence for five years
obligations.plain: An operator must post the main contents of its risk-management, explanation, and user-protection measures, plus the name and contact details of the human supervisor, at its office or on its website. It must retain supporting documents for the Article 34 measures for five years; trade secrets may be omitted from the public posting, but the retention duty remains.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to operators of high-impact AI or products or services using it.

evidence: Website or premises copy of the published measures and supervisor contact details
Five-year retention schedule and supporting-document repository
obligations.penalty: No standalone administrative fine is specified for a breach of Article 34 measures; MSIT may investigate and order correction, and failure to comply with a corrective order can incur up to KRW 30 million under Act Article 43(1)(3). MSIT announced a minimum one-year enforcement grace.
obligations.notes: The Decree permits trade-secret material to be excluded from public posting. It also deems some measures implemented by an AI-using operator where the upstream system is received without significant functional change; see Decree Art. 27(3).
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Enforcement Decree Enforcement Decree Art. 27(1)-(2); Act Art. 34(1)

obligations.title: Endeavor to assess fundamental-rights impacts of high-impact AI
obligations.plain: An operator providing products or services using high-impact AI must endeavor to assess in advance the impact on people's fundamental rights. The Decree lists assessment elements including affected people and rights, social and economic effects, use patterns, evaluation metrics, risk prevention or mitigation, loss recovery, and improvement plans.

applies_to.conditions: The Act frames the operator's assessment duty as an effort duty; public bodies separately must prioritize products or services that have undergone an assessment.

evidence: Completed or planned impact assessment with affected groups, rights, risks, and mitigations
Written rationale and action plan for any identified improvements
obligations.notes: Article 35(1) says the operator shall endeavor to assess; it is not a categorical duty to complete an assessment in every case.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 35(1); Enforcement Decree Art. 28

obligations.article: Art. 35(1) second sentence; Enforcement Decree Art. 28(1)(1)
obligations.title: Reflect AI-vulnerable groups in impact assessments
obligations.plain: When an operator carries out an impact assessment for high-impact AI, the assessment must reflect the characteristics of AI-vulnerable groups, taking account of the nature of the product or service. The amended sentence took effect on 21 July 2026.

applies_to.conditions: Applies when an operator performs the Article 35 impact assessment; the assessment must account for vulnerable-group characteristics in light of the product or service.

evidence: Assessment materials identifying relevant vulnerable groups and how their characteristics were considered
Records linking assessment findings to mitigation or improvement measures
obligations.notes: The amendment was enacted by Act No. 21311 on 20 January 2026; this part became effective six months later, on 21 July 2026.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 35(1) second sentence; Enforcement Decree Art. 28(1)(1)

obligations.title: Prefer high-impact AI products or services with impact assessments
obligations.plain: When State agencies and other covered public institutions intend to use products or services using high-impact AI, they must give priority consideration to products or services that have undergone an impact assessment.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to covered State agencies, local governments, and public institutions procuring or using high-impact AI products or services.

evidence: Procurement or use decision record showing how impact-assessed options received priority consideration

obligations.title: Appoint a domestic agent when foreign-operator thresholds are met
obligations.plain: An AI business operator without an address or place of business in Korea must designate a domestic agent in writing and report the designation to MSIT if it meets any Decree threshold: prior-year total revenue of at least KRW 1 trillion; prior-year AI-service revenue of at least KRW 10 billion; at least one million average daily domestic users over the preceding three months as of the previous year-end; or an administrative fine for failing to comply with a corrective order. The agent handles specified safety-result submissions, high-impact classification requests, and support for Article 34 measures; the operator is treated as responsible for the agent's related violations.

applies_to.conditions: No Korean address or business office and at least one Article 29 threshold; the fourth trigger is a prior administrative fine under Act Article 43(1)(3).

evidence: Written domestic-agent appointment and report to MSIT
Annual threshold assessment covering revenue, AI-service revenue, Korean user counts, and any relevant fine
obligations.penalty: Up to KRW 30 million administrative fine for failure to designate an agent under Article 43(1)(2); MSIT announced that penalties are deferred during an enforcement grace period of at least one year, subject to highly exceptional cases.
obligations.notes: The decree includes an additional trigger for an operator fined for failure to comply with an MSIT corrective order. Revenue values for foreign operators are converted into Korean won using the prior-year average exchange rate.
obligations.cite: AI Basic Act Art. 36(1)-(3); Enforcement Decree Art. 29

obligations.title: Make AI decision processes explainable, fair and human-centric
obligations.plain: The voluntary second-edition framework recommends explainable, transparent and fair AI decision-making, with human well-being and safety central to design, development and deployment. It is guidance, not a legal duty.

applies_to.conditions: Organisations deploying AI should tailor the framework's recommendations to their risks and context.

evidence: Decision-process documentation and records of human-centered design and fairness review

obligations.title: Govern Generative AI across its lifecycle and ecosystem
obligations.plain: The voluntary framework recommends an ecosystem approach spanning accountability, data, trusted development and deployment, incident reporting, testing and assurance, security, content provenance, safety and alignment research, and AI for public good. It creates no statutory compliance duty.

applies_to.conditions: Organizations across the Generative AI ecosystem; recommendations are voluntary.

evidence: Governance records showing lifecycle risk, testing, security, incident and provenance practices
obligations.notes: IMDA's official 2024 annual report confirms the nine dimensions and the voluntary nature of its model frameworks.
obligations.cite: Generative AI Governance Framework (2024) Framework, nine dimensions

obligations.title: Bound agent risks before deployment
obligations.plain: The framework recommends assessing whether an agent use case is suitable, then limiting its access to tools and systems and defining its identity, permissions and scope of actions. The appropriate boundary should reflect the risk and reversibility of agent actions.

applies_to.conditions: Guidance for organizations developing agents in-house or deploying third-party agentic solutions.

evidence: Agent risk assessment, tool allowlist and permission-scope configuration

obligations.title: Assign accountable humans and approval checkpoints
obligations.plain: The framework recommends clear allocation of responsibility across internal teams and external vendors, with meaningful human oversight. Significant checkpoints should require human approval, especially for high-stakes or irreversible agent actions.

applies_to.conditions: Guidance for organizations developing or deploying agentic systems.

evidence: Named accountable owners, checkpoint rules and approval records for consequential actions

obligations.title: Test, monitor and log agent behavior
obligations.plain: The framework recommends technical controls throughout the agent lifecycle, including pre-deployment testing and continuous monitoring and testing after deployment. It also recommends reporting and failsafe mechanisms for agent failures or unexpected behavior.

applies_to.conditions: Guidance for organizations developing or deploying agentic systems.

evidence: Pre-deployment test results, attributable action logs, monitoring records and agent-failure runbook

obligations.title: Inform and train agent end users
obligations.plain: The framework recommends telling users about an agent's range of actions, its data access and the user's responsibilities. Organizations should consider training employees to manage human-agent interactions, provide effective oversight and retain relevant skills.

applies_to.conditions: Guidance for organizations whose staff or customers interact with or integrate agents into work processes.

evidence: User-facing notice of agent capabilities and training materials for staff

obligations.title: Test AI systems against responsible-AI principles
obligations.plain: AI Verify is an optional testing framework and software toolkit for assessing AI systems against 11 governance principles. It combines standardized tests for selected properties with process checks, and current IMDA materials describe coverage for both traditional AI and Generative AI.

applies_to.conditions: Optional assurance tool; it is not a statutory certification requirement.

evidence: AI Verify assessment results and supporting test records
obligations.cite: AI Verify Testing Framework, 11 governance principles

obligations.title: Do not publish realistic false candidate representations in online election ads
obligations.plain: During an election period, publishing or causing publication in Singapore of online election advertising with a digitally generated or manipulated audio, visual or audiovisual representation that realistically depicts a candidate saying or doing something they did not is an offence. The law contains specific exceptions, including private or domestic communications and publication of election news by an authorized news agency.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to relevant online election advertising published in Singapore during the election period, where the publisher knows or ought reasonably to know its election-advertising character.

evidence: Election-period content review and approval records for online political advertising
obligations.penalty: Fine up to S$1,000, imprisonment up to 12 months, or both, on conviction.

obligations.title: Establish a lawful basis and notify purposes for personal-data use
obligations.plain: An organization must not collect, use or disclose personal data unless consent, deemed consent, an applicable exception or another law permits it. It must limit use to appropriate purposes and notify individuals as required; these duties apply when personal data is processed for AI development or deployment.

applies_to.conditions: An organization collects, uses or discloses personal data in an AI system or model.

evidence: Consent or exception records and notices that identify the purposes of AI-related personal-data processing
obligations.penalty: PDPA directions and financial penalties may apply under section 48J; the applicable cap depends on the contravention and organization.

obligations.title: Maintain accountability, security and retention controls
obligations.plain: Organizations must take responsibility for personal data under their control, maintain data-protection policies and practices, make reasonable security arrangements, and cease retaining personal data when retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes. These duties also apply to personal data used in AI systems.

applies_to.conditions: An organization holds or controls personal data processed in an AI context.

evidence: Data-protection policies, security controls and retention schedules for AI-related personal data

obligations.title: Apply PDPC's advice to AI recommendation and decision systems
obligations.plain: The nonbinding guidelines explain how the PDPA applies to personal data used to develop and deploy machine-learning systems that make recommendations, predictions or decisions. They recommend meaningful consent, contextual notices and proportionate transparency about relevant data use and safeguards.

applies_to.conditions: Personal data is used in an AI recommendation, prediction or decision system; underlying PDPA duties remain binding.

evidence: AI data-use assessment and consumer-facing notice describing relevant data and purposes
obligations.notes: PDPC states the guidelines are advisory and not legally binding; the PDPA itself remains binding.
obligations.instrument_short: PDPC AI Recommendation and Decision Guidelines
obligations.cite: PDPC AI Recommendation and Decision Guidelines Guidelines §§ 2.2, 3.1, 9.1-9.7 and 10

obligations.title: Give AI-specific notices for large-scale GenAI training data
obligations.plain: The advisory guidance says general notifications are insufficient for large-scale Generative AI model training or fine-tuning and recommends AI-specific notices describing the data and its use. It also encourages data minimization or anonymization and confirms that model providers processing personal data are organizations under the PDPA.

applies_to.conditions: Use of personal data in Generative AI development or deployment; the AI-specific notice point concerns large-scale training or fine-tuning.

evidence: AI-specific training notice, data-minimization record and privacy controls for model development
obligations.notes: The guidance is advisory and nonbinding; the underlying PDPA consent, notification and protection duties remain binding.
obligations.cite: PDPC Generative AI Guidelines Guidelines §§ 4.2-4.8, 5.1 and 7.1

obligations.title: Do not communicate qualifying intimate or child-abuse images
obligations.plain: The Act prohibits communications that meet the statutory definitions of intimate-image abuse or image-based child abuse; the relevant image definitions include images altered or generated by any means. These harms are in the first operational phase, and victims may seek civil remedies while the Commissioner may direct communicators, administrators or platforms to act.

applies_to.conditions: Only material meeting the statutory thresholds and exceptions; the Act's first-phase harms became operational on 29 June 2026.

evidence: Content review, notice escalation and removal records for qualifying harmful image material
obligations.penalty: Victims may seek civil remedies; the Commissioner may issue directions under the Act.
obligations.notes: MDDI confirmed AI-generated content is within scope where it meets the thresholds for the implemented harms. Official response: https://www.mddi.gov.sg/newsroom/mddi-response-to-pq-on-protecting-against-unauthorised-ai-generated-likeness-in-advertisements-and-operationalising-online-safety-commission-mandate-over-inauthentic-material-abuse/.

obligations.title: Track the pending inauthentic-material-abuse provisions
obligations.plain: Section 16 covers online inauthentic material abuse, including realistic false or misleading digitally altered or generated depictions that meet the statutory harm threshold; section 86 provides the corresponding tort. MDDI said this category would be progressively implemented and had not announced a commencement date as of 10 September 2026.

applies_to.conditions: Not yet operational as of 4 November 2026; monitor for a commencement notification.

evidence: Monitor official commencement announcements and retain a content-response plan for realistic AI depictions
obligations.notes: MDDI's 10 September 2026 response stated that inauthentic material abuse would be progressively implemented and that further commencement details would follow.

obligations.title: Publish and maintain a frontier safety framework
obligations.plain: A large frontier developer must write, implement, follow and clearly publish a frontier AI framework covering catastrophic-risk assessment, mitigations, governance, cybersecurity and safe deployment. It must review the framework at least annually, update it as needed, and publish a summary of material changes with reasons within 30 days.

applies_to.conditions: A frontier model is a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, including original training and qualifying later fine-tuning or modification. A large frontier developer is a developer together with affiliates whose preceding-year annual gross revenue exceeds $500 million.

evidence: Publicly accessible, dated frontier AI framework and change history
Annual review record and documented catastrophic-risk assessments and mitigations
obligations.penalty: Civil penalties may reach $1,000,000 per violation for specified violations by a large frontier developer.
obligations.notes: The $500 million revenue test applies to the developer and affiliates together; the compute threshold includes qualifying later training or modification.

obligations.title: Publish deployment reports and report critical safety incidents
obligations.plain: Before or concurrently with deployment of a new or substantially modified frontier model, a frontier developer must publish a transparency report with specified release, contact, capability, use and restriction information; large developers add specified risk-assessment and evaluation information. A developer must report a critical safety incident to the Office of Emergency Services within 15 days after discovery, or notify an appropriate authority within 24 hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury; large developers also transmit confidential summaries of internal-use catastrophic-risk assessments to OES quarterly or on an alternate schedule communicated in writing.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to developers of models exceeding the statutory 10^26-compute frontier-model threshold; the enhanced report and internal-use assessment requirements apply to large frontier developers exceeding the $500 million preceding-year revenue threshold.

evidence: Published, dated deployment transparency reports and quarterly confidential internal-use assessment summaries, where applicable
Incident register with discovery, escalation and OES/authority notification timestamps
obligations.penalty: Civil penalties and other statutory remedies apply; specified large-developer violations may incur up to $1,000,000 per violation.
obligations.notes: The 24-hour urgent notification and the 15-day OES reporting requirements are distinct. OES receives confidential internal-use assessment summaries from large developers on the applicable schedule.

obligations.title: Provide a free generative-AI disclosure verification tool
obligations.plain: A covered provider must make a free, publicly accessible tool available to determine whether image, video or audio content was created or altered using its generative-AI system. The tool must expose the specified provenance information while limiting personal-information collection and retention as the statute requires.

applies_to.conditions: Covers providers of publicly accessible generative-AI systems in California, subject to statutory exceptions, including a temporary assistive-technology exemption. SB 1000, effective 2026-09-30, removed the former more-than-one-million-monthly-user threshold.

evidence: Public link and test records for the free provenance-verification tool
Technical and privacy documentation showing required provenance data and minimized data handling
obligations.penalty: Generally $5,000 per violation per day.
obligations.notes: The user's lead about a one-million-user threshold is outdated. SB 1000 removed that threshold and deleted the optional manifest-disclosure route; the current tool duty is not limited to providers above that user count.

obligations.title: Embed latent provenance disclosures in generated or altered media
obligations.plain: Where technically feasible, a provider must embed a latent disclosure in image, video and audio content created or altered by its generative-AI system, except for specified minor modifications. The disclosure must identify the AI origin and include the information prescribed by statute; providers must also give licensees required notice and act on identified noncompliant modifications within the statutory time limits.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to covered generative-AI providers when latent disclosure is technically feasible; minor modifications and the temporary assistive-technology exemption are excluded as specified by statute.

evidence: Sample image, video and audio outputs with inspectable latent provenance disclosures
Feasibility assessment and licensee notices, compliance escalations and remediation records
obligations.penalty: Generally $5,000 per violation per day; specified false claims of assistive-technology exemption carry a separate higher penalty until 2029-01-01.
obligations.notes: SB 1000 removed the former manifest-disclosure option. The latent-disclosure requirement is limited by technical feasibility and the statute's enumerated exceptions.

obligations.title: Detect and disclose provenance on large platforms and GenAI hosting services
obligations.plain: From 2027-01-01, a large online platform must provide a compliant mechanism to detect provenance data, display the prescribed indicator or disclosure, and permit inspection; it must take reasonable steps not to strip compliant provenance. A GenAI hosting platform must not knowingly make a covered system available if it does not comply with the latent-disclosure requirements, and platforms need not maintain, display or enable downloading of users' personal information as provenance.

applies_to.conditions: A large online platform is a public-facing social-media, file-sharing, mass-messaging or stand-alone search platform that distributes content to users who did not create or collaborate on it and exceeded 2,000,000 unique monthly users during the preceding 12 months, excluding broadband and telecommunications services. A GenAI hosting platform is an internet website or application making model weights or source code available for download by California residents, regardless of compensation. Platform duties concern provenance data compliant with widely adopted specifications of an established standards-setting body.

evidence: Provenance-detection, inspection and user-interface tests against compliant interoperable standards; policies and logs for avoiding removal of provenance data
Hosting-service checks that covered systems comply with latent-disclosure requirements
obligations.penalty: Generally $5,000 per violation per day.
obligations.notes: AB 2713 revised detection, interface, inspection and no-stripping requirements. The platform is not required to preserve or disclose personal information as part of the provenance mechanism.

obligations.title: Support provenance disclosures in newly manufactured capture devices
obligations.plain: Beginning 2028-01-01, a manufacturer of a covered capture device first produced for sale in California must provide an option to include and, where required, embed a latent disclosure identifying the manufacturer, device, version and capture date or time. The duty is subject to technical feasibility and the statute's accepted technical specifications.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to covered image, video and audio capture devices first manufactured for sale in California on or after 2028-01-01, subject to statutory technical-feasibility and specification conditions.

evidence: Device technical specifications and provenance options
Test captures demonstrating default embedding where technically required
obligations.penalty: Generally $5,000 per violation per day.
obligations.notes: This is a later phase-in than the provider tool and latent-disclosure duties.

obligations.title: Publish generative-AI training-data documentation
obligations.plain: A developer must publish documentation about the datasets used to develop a covered generative-AI system or service, including a high-level summary of source types, dataset purpose and characteristics, intellectual-property and personal-information content, processing, collection periods and use of synthetic data. The documentation must be posted publicly online by the initial deadline and updated before a subsequent release or substantial modification, subject to statutory exceptions.

applies_to.conditions: Covers generative-AI systems or services released on or after 2022 and made available to Californians; statutory exceptions include specified systems and circumstances.

evidence: Public training-data documentation with the required dataset categories
Version history showing publication and updates before later releases or substantial modifications
obligations.penalty: No standalone penalty amount is specified in § 3111.
obligations.notes: Initial public documentation was due 2026-01-01; it is an ongoing publication duty before subsequent covered release or substantial modification.

obligations.title: Disclose companion-chatbot identity and maintain crisis and minor safeguards
obligations.plain: A companion-chatbot operator must disclose when a reasonable person could be misled into believing the chatbot is human, maintain and publish a protocol for responding to suicidal ideation or self-harm, and provide a notice that the chatbot may not be suitable for some minors. Until 2027-01-01, the statute also requires specified disclosures, break reminders and protections for known minor users; SB 1119 repeals those § 22602(c) duties from that date.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to operators of companion chatbots made available to users in California; a companion chatbot is designed to provide adaptive, human-like responses and sustain a relationship across multiple interactions.

evidence: User-facing human-mimicry and minor-suitability notices; published suicidal-ideation and self-harm protocol with tested escalation paths
Records of known-minor disclosures and break reminders through 2026-12-31
obligations.penalty: Civil penalties and other statutory remedies apply; exact exposure depends on the provision and violation.
obligations.notes: The known-minor requirements in § 22602(c) are operative as of 2026-11-04 but are scheduled for deletion by SB 1119 effective 2027-01-01. Do not treat them as a permanent duty after that date.

obligations.title: Report companion-chatbot safety and crisis-response information annually
obligations.plain: An operator must submit an annual report stating the number of notifications sent to users about suicidal ideation or self-harm during the preceding calendar year and describing protocols for detecting, removing or responding to such content. Reports must avoid personally identifying information and include specified safety and use information.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to operators of companion chatbots subject to the Act; the first annual report is due 2027-07-01 and covers the preceding calendar year as required by statute.

evidence: Annual report and submission receipt with aggregated notification counts and documented crisis-response procedures
Privacy review showing report data excludes personally identifying information
obligations.penalty: Civil penalties and other statutory remedies apply.
obligations.notes: The duty is a 2027 phase-in; it should not be represented as an already-due report on the as-of date.

obligations.title: Assess and mitigate child-safety risks in AI chatbots
obligations.plain: From 2027-01-01, operators must determine users' ages or apply child protections to all users. From 2027-07-01, before new or substantially modified releases, operators allowing children must document a safety risk assessment and mitigations, publish a safety policy and crisis procedures, and implement required safeguards, defaults and data or advertising restrictions. Under § 21814's AB 1405-conditioned text, operators with at least $500 million in prior-year gross revenue must complete an independent audit by 2029-01-01 or before first public availability (whichever is later), then every two years, submit an audit summary to the Attorney General within 30 business days and post a high-level summary within 90 days; operators below that threshold are exempt before 2032.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to covered operators of AI chatbots accessible to children, subject to statutory definitions and exclusions, including specified workplace-exclusive and postsecondary educational chatbots. The child-safety risk-assessment, mitigation and policy duties begin 2027-07-01; audit requirements have revenue thresholds, small-operator provisions and an exemption/phase-in before 2032.

evidence: Age-assurance implementation and records of applicable user-protection defaults
Child-safety assessments, mitigation plans, policies, crisis procedures, safeguard tests and independent audit reports/remediation where § 21814 applies
obligations.penalty: Civil penalties may be imposed per affected child, with higher amounts for intentional violations; statutory enforcement and remedies also apply.
obligations.notes: AB 1405 was chaptered on 2026-09-09 and, absent a special effective-date clause, takes effect 2027-01-01; accordingly, SB 1119's alternate § 21814 text conditioned on AB 1405 being chaptered and effective by that date is the applicable version. Under that text, operators with less than $500 million in prior-year gross revenue are exempt from audit duties before 2032; audit summaries go to the Attorney General within 30 business days and high-level public summaries within 90 days. SB 1119 also removes BPC § 22602(c) minor-specific companion-chatbot provisions effective 2027-01-01.

obligations.title: Disclose a qualifying bot's artificial identity
obligations.plain: A person using a bot online must clearly and conspicuously disclose that it is a bot when the person intends to mislead someone about the bot's artificial identity, knowingly deceive that person about the communication's content, and thereby incentivize a commercial transaction or influence a vote in an election. The disclosure must be reasonably designed to inform people that they are communicating with a bot.

applies_to.conditions: Narrowly applies to the combination of intent to mislead about artificial identity, knowing deception about the communication's content, and an aim to incentivize a commercial transaction or influence an election; statutory exceptions apply.

evidence: Disclosure shown in the qualifying online interaction
Records explaining the deployment purpose and applicable statutory exception analysis
obligations.penalty: Civil enforcement remedies are available under the Act.
obligations.notes: This is not a general chatbot-disclosure rule; all statutory intent and purpose elements must be present.

obligations.title: Complete CCPA risk assessments for high-risk processing
obligations.plain: A CCPA-covered business must conduct and document a risk assessment before initiating processing that presents significant risk to consumers, including selling or sharing personal information, processing sensitive personal information, using ADMT for a significant decision, specified profiling, and using personal information to train covered technologies. A covered business already conducting qualifying processing before the regulations took effect must complete the assessment by 2027-12-31 if that processing continues; required information and attestations for 2026–2027 assessments are due 2028-04-01.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to businesses subject to the CCPA that engage in processing identified by the risk-assessment regulations; statutory business, processing and decision exceptions apply.

evidence: Dated risk assessments completed before initiation of new covered processing and for qualifying legacy processing, with approvals and mitigations
Submission receipt and executive attestation for the 2026–2027 reporting period
obligations.penalty: CCPA enforcement penalties and remedies may apply; amounts depend on violation and circumstances.
obligations.notes: The regulations' risk-assessment duties apply from 2026-01-01; this obligation is distinct from the later ADMT access, notice and opt-out rights.
obligations.cite: CPPA ADMT and risk assessments 11 CCR § 7150 and related risk-assessment provisions

obligations.title: Give notice, opt-out and access rights for covered ADMT
obligations.plain: From 2027-01-01, a CCPA-covered business using covered ADMT for a significant decision must provide a prominent pre-use notice explaining the purpose, operation and consumer rights. Consumers generally have an opt-out right, subject to regulatory exceptions including certain qualifying human-appeal processes, and may request a plain-language explanation of the specific ADMT use, logic and role in the decision.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to CCPA-covered businesses using ADMT as defined by regulation to make or substantially replace human decisionmaking for a significant decision, subject to statutory and regulatory exclusions and exceptions.

evidence: Prominent pre-use notices and plain-language access explanations describing purpose, logic, output and decision role
Functional opt-out and qualifying appeal workflows, with request-handling logs
obligations.penalty: CCPA enforcement penalties and remedies may apply; amounts depend on violation and circumstances.
obligations.notes: The specific opt-out exceptions and implementation alternatives are regulatory; verify that an exception's conditions are met before relying on it.
obligations.cite: CPPA ADMT and risk assessments 11 CCR §§ 7200–7222

obligations.title: Prevent discriminatory employment use of automated decision systems
obligations.plain: An employer or other FEHA-covered entity may not use an automated-decision system or selection criteria that discriminates against applicants or employees on a protected basis. Anti-bias testing or its absence is relevant evidence in a discrimination claim or defense, while covered personnel and employment records must be retained for four years from record creation or the personnel action, whichever is later.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to FEHA-covered employers and other covered entities using automated-decision systems or selection criteria in employment decisions; the regulations do not impose a freestanding universal anti-bias-testing mandate.

evidence: Employment ADS and selection-criteria inventory, anti-bias testing or rationale, and documented response to results
Personnel and employment records with a four-year retention schedule under § 11013(c)
obligations.penalty: FEHA administrative and civil remedies may apply; case-specific.
obligations.notes: The final regulation makes testing evidence relevant to claims and defenses, not an independent testing mandate. CRD's official effective-date announcement confirms 2025-10-01 and the four-year retention period, but the PDF text extraction merges the deleted word "two" with inserted "four," so exact codified wording should be rechecked against the final formatted rule.

obligations.title: Require human corroboration and notice for workplace automated decisions
obligations.plain: From 2027-07-01, covered employers may not rely solely on an automated decision system to discipline or terminate an employee, and must corroborate specified outputs with a human when those outputs are primarily relied upon. Employers must give employees notice after covered use and provide a description of relevant data on request; the Act also prohibits specified uses of automated systems in employment decisions.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to employers and automated decision systems as defined in SB 947 for covered employees; statutory exceptions include specified collective-bargaining, national-security and other circumstances.

evidence: Human corroboration records, employee notices and data-description response records
Screening records for prohibited automated-decision uses and applicable exceptions
obligations.penalty: $500 per violation, in addition to other available remedies.
obligations.notes: These duties are enacted but not operative on the 2026-11-04 as-of date.
obligations.cite: Worker protections for automated decisions Labor Code §§ 1522, 1524 and 1526.7

obligations.title: Use reasonable care and document high-risk systems
obligations.plain: Developers of high-risk AI systems must use reasonable care to protect consumers from known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination and provide downstream deployers with required system documentation. The original law also requires disclosure of discovered algorithmic discrimination to the Attorney General and known downstream developers or deployers within 90 days.

applies_to.conditions: High-risk AI systems making or substantially influencing a consequential decision; these predecessor duties apply during the transition before 2027-01-01.

evidence: Documented risk analysis and system/deployer documentation for each covered high-risk system
Record of any discovered algorithmic discrimination and timely notice to the Attorney General and known downstream parties
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally; a federal court order restricts the Attorney General's initiation of enforcement for covered violations, without changing statutory applicability dates.
obligations.notes: SB 25B-004 moved the original implementation date to 2026-06-30. SB 26-189's general effective date is 2027-01-01, so the 2024 duties remain in the statutory transition through 2026-12-31. The April 27, 2026 federal minute order bars the Attorney General from initiating enforcement, including investigations, for alleged violations of SB 24-205 or its 2026 replacement occurring on or before 14 days after the court rules on xAI's forthcoming preliminary-injunction motion. It does not change statutory dates. The order names the Attorney General defendant; the 2024 statute also permits district-attorney enforcement. The rulemaking was not final as of 2026-11-04. Order PDF: https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cod.253513/gov.uscourts.cod.253513.24.0.pdf

obligations.title: Run risk management and impact assessments for high-risk AI
obligations.plain: Deployers of high-risk AI systems must use reasonable care to protect consumers from algorithmic-discrimination risks and implement a risk-management policy and program. They must complete an impact assessment before deployment and at least annually, and within 90 days after an intentional and substantial modification, subject to statutory exceptions.

applies_to.conditions: High-risk AI systems making or substantially influencing consequential decisions; predecessor duties apply only until the successor framework takes effect on 2027-01-01.

evidence: Risk-management policy and program with owners, processes, mitigations, and review history
Initial and annual impact assessments, plus assessments after substantial modifications
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.
obligations.notes: The delayed 2024 framework remains applicable during the transition period; it is not the successor law's standard. AG enforcement is subject to the temporary federal order described in the SB 24-205 instrument's first obligation.

obligations.title: Notify consumers and publish high-risk system information
obligations.plain: Deployers must provide the required consumer notice when a high-risk system is used for a consequential decision and publish a statement describing the types of high-risk systems they deploy and how they manage known algorithmic-discrimination risks. The statement must be updated at least annually, subject to statutory exceptions.

applies_to.conditions: High-risk AI systems deployed to make or substantially influence consequential decisions; predecessor duties apply until 2027-01-01.

evidence: Consumer notices and a current public statement describing covered systems and risk management
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.

obligations.title: Mark and disclose synthetic content
obligations.plain: Developers of covered systems that generate or manipulate synthetic digital content must provide a machine-readable marker, to the extent technically feasible, and deployers must disclose to consumers that content is artificially generated or manipulated. This is a predecessor duty scheduled to be replaced on 2027-01-01.

applies_to.conditions: Systems that generate or manipulate synthetic digital content, subject to the statutory exceptions.

evidence: Description and test results for machine-readable output marking
Consumer-facing labels for synthetic media
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.
obligations.notes: The successor SB 26-189 framework does not impose these same general synthetic-content marking duties; this obligation is included only for the transitional SB 24-205 period ending 2026-12-31.

obligations.title: Give deployers usable documentation for covered ADMT
obligations.plain: Developers must provide each deployer with an understandable statement of intended and known harmful uses, known training-data categories, limitations and risks, instructions for appropriate use, monitoring and meaningful human review, and information reasonably needed for deployer disclosures. They must give timely notice of material updates, substantial modifications, or changes to intended use, limitations, or risk mitigation; the detailed documentation duties apply only to uses marketed, advertised, configured, contracted, sold, or licensed for consequential decisions.

applies_to.conditions: A covered ADMT materially influences a consequential decision in education, employment, housing, financial/lending services, insurance, health-care services, or essential government services; statutory definition excludes specified ordinary tools and human-review-only tasks.

evidence: Developer documentation supplied to each deployer, including use limits, data categories, risks, and review instructions
Versioned change log and direct notices of material updates to deployers
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally; the SB 26-189 enforcement and cure provisions apply.
obligations.notes: The statute requires technical documentation, not a general algorithmic impact assessment. The draft AG rules may clarify scope and content but were not adopted as of 2026-11-04. AG enforcement is also subject to the temporary federal order noted above.

obligations.title: Keep developer and deployer compliance records
obligations.plain: Developers must retain records reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance for at least three years after creating each record. Deployers must retain records reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance for at least three years after the consequential decision, including relevant system-version, change-log, and mitigation records.

applies_to.conditions: Covered ADMT used to materially influence a consequential decision; longer retention applies when required by other law.

evidence: Retention schedule and records linking decisions to system versions and mitigation changes
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.

obligations.title: Tell consumers before covered ADMT influences a decision
obligations.plain: Before using covered ADMT to materially influence a consequential decision, a deployer must give the consumer clear and conspicuous notice that the decision uses ADMT and instructions for obtaining further information. A prominent public notice reasonably accessible near consumer interactions may satisfy this requirement.

applies_to.conditions: The covered ADMT materially influences a consequential decision affecting the consumer; housing is also a covered domain.

evidence: Consumer-facing notice and records showing it was available before use at relevant interaction points
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally; AG enforcement only for this statutory duty.

obligations.title: Explain the ADMT role after an adverse outcome
obligations.plain: Within 30 days after an adverse outcome, the deployer must give a plain-language description of the consequential decision and ADMT's role, a simple process for requesting more information about the system and inputs, and an explanation of the consumer's data-correction and human-review rights. The statute does not itself require a full individualized rationale for why the outcome occurred; federal-law, trade-secret, and other statutory limits apply.

applies_to.conditions: A covered ADMT materially influences a consequential decision that results in an adverse outcome for a consumer; housing is also a covered domain.

evidence: Adverse-outcome notice template and dated evidence of delivery within 30 days
Process for consumers to request system and input information and exercise statutory rights
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally; 60-day cure if the Attorney General deems a cure possible, except knowing or repeated violations.
obligations.notes: Proposed 4 CCR 904-6 rules would further specify disclosure content, but were not final as of 2026-11-04. The statute requires a description of the decision and ADMT's role, not a free-standing explanation of the adverse decision's substantive merits.

obligations.title: Offer data correction and meaningful human review on request
obligations.plain: After an adverse outcome materially influenced by covered ADMT, a consumer may request instructions for accessing and correcting factually incorrect or materially inaccurate personal data used in the decision, plus an opportunity for meaningful human review and reconsideration to the extent commercially reasonable. The right does not require correction of opinions, predictions, scores, or protected evaluations; education deployers subject to FERPA may use existing compliant processes.

applies_to.conditions: Consumer experienced an adverse outcome from a consequential decision materially influenced by covered ADMT; meaningful review is subject to commercial reasonableness and statutory exceptions.

evidence: Consumer request and correction/review workflow with a trained human reviewer
Record of review, reconsideration, and response to the consumer
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally; 60-day cure if the Attorney General deems a cure possible, except knowing or repeated violations.
obligations.notes: This is a request right after an adverse outcome, not a general appeal right for every automated decision. The Act does not require a general impact assessment or deployer risk-management program; those were present in SB 24-205 but are not in the successor ADMT duties. The Attorney General's rules clarifying consumer rights were due by 2027-01-01 and remained proposed as of 2026-11-04.

obligations.title: Estimate ages and protect minor chatbot users
obligations.plain: Operators must use commercially reasonable or generally accepted methods to estimate account-holder and user ages and may not willfully disregard clear and convincing evidence that a person is a minor. When the operator knows a user is a minor, it must give the required AI disclosure, avoid unpredictable engagement rewards, use technically feasible protections against specified sexual content and intimate depictions, take reasonable measures against simulated emotional dependence, stop explicit sexual exchanges, comply with minor-privacy duties, and provide privacy and account controls to minors and their parents or guardians.

applies_to.conditions: Operator develops and makes publicly available or offers a conversational AI service accessible to the general public that primarily simulates human conversation; minor means under 18, and an estimated age/range is treated as knowledge.

evidence: Age-estimation method and records of decisions about known or estimated minor status
Minor safety controls, privacy settings, parent/guardian tools, and testing records
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.
obligations.notes: Statutory exceptions exclude specified narrow-topic, business-internal, virtual-assistant, or other services; check the definition of conversational AI service and operator before applying.

obligations.title: Disclose that a conversational AI service is AI
obligations.plain: Operators must clearly and conspicuously tell users that the service is artificial intelligence. The disclosure must appear at the beginning of the user's first interaction each calendar day, at least once every three hours in a continuous interaction or persistently on screen, and in response to a user's question about whether it is AI rather than human.

applies_to.conditions: Operators of covered conversational AI services; separate disclosure format applies to known minor users under § 6-1-1708(2)(a).

evidence: Screenshots or transcripts showing first-session, recurring or persistent, and responsive disclosures
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.

obligations.title: Respond to suicide and self-harm prompts and report annually
obligations.plain: Operators must implement a protocol for responses to user prompts about suicidal ideation or self-harm, including referral to an appropriate crisis service (not law enforcement) and escalation for repeated or severe indicators. Beginning 2027-07-01, operators must report annually to the Attorney General the referral count, relevant protocols and AG-requested efficacy metrics, without user identifiers or personal information, using evidence-based measurement methods.

applies_to.conditions: Operators of covered conversational AI services; the first annual reporting date is 2027-07-01 and the report must not contain user identifiers or personal information.

evidence: Crisis-response protocol, referral and escalation logs, and annual-report submission
Evidence-based self-harm measurement method and privacy review confirming reports contain no user identifiers
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.

obligations.title: Do not misrepresent chatbot outputs as professional services
obligations.plain: Operators may not knowingly or recklessly state that chatbot output is provided by, endorsed by, or equivalent to services provided by a licensed health-care or legal professional, a licensed/certified/registered mental-health professional, or a qualified dietitian.

applies_to.conditions: Operators of covered conversational AI services.

evidence: Marketing and in-product claims review for professional-equivalence representations
obligations.penalty: Up to $20,000 per violation under the CCPA generally.

obligations.title: Do not use discriminatory AI in employment
obligations.plain: In covered recruitment, hiring, promotion, renewal, training/apprenticeship selection, discharge, discipline, tenure, or employment-terms decisions, an employer commits a civil-rights violation by using AI that has the effect of subjecting employees to discrimination based on an IHRA-protected class or by using ZIP codes as a proxy for protected classes.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to employers and employment practices enumerated in §2-102(L); the prohibition addresses discriminatory effect and ZIP-code proxies, not every use of AI in employment.

evidence: Employment-model impact testing across relevant protected classes and ZIP-code proxy review
Documented model-use decision and corrective-action records

obligations.title: Notify employees when covered AI is used
obligations.plain: An employer commits a civil-rights violation if it fails to notify an employee that it is using AI for the employment purposes listed in §2-102(L)(1). The statute delegates notice circumstances, timing, and means to IDHR rulemaking; the Department's proposed amendments were withdrawn, so the withdrawn draft's details are not encoded as binding requirements.

applies_to.conditions: Notice is required for AI use in the enumerated employment practices; the Act itself leaves the timing and means to IDHR rules.

evidence: Employee notice template describing the employer's covered AI use
Notice delivery or acknowledgement record
obligations.notes: The June 26, 2026 JCAR Flinn Report records IDHR's withdrawal of its proposed rule amendments. Do not use the withdrawn draft's proposed notice timing, form, or record-retention provisions as operative law.

obligations.title: Disclose, explain, and obtain consent before AI video analysis
obligations.plain: Before asking an applicant to submit a video interview for an Illinois-based position, an employer using AI analysis must tell the applicant AI may analyze the video and assess fitness, explain how the AI works and the general characteristics it evaluates, and obtain the applicant's consent. The employer may not use AI to evaluate an applicant who has not consented.

applies_to.conditions: Applies only when the employer asks applicants to record video interviews and uses AI analysis of applicant-submitted video for positions based in Illinois.

evidence: Pre-interview AI disclosure and plain-language explanation
Applicant's affirmative consent record before analysis

obligations.title: Limit video sharing and delete interviews on request
obligations.plain: An employer may share an applicant's interview video only with people whose expertise or technology is necessary to evaluate fitness for the position. Within 30 days after an applicant's request, the employer must delete the interview and instruct recipients to delete their copies, including electronic backups.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to applicant-submitted videos analyzed under the Act; recipient deletion instructions and backup copies are included.

evidence: Vendor/recipient access list limited to necessary evaluation expertise or technology
Deletion request log and recipient/back-up deletion confirmations within 30 days

obligations.title: Report demographic data for AI-only video screening
obligations.plain: An employer that relies solely on AI analysis of a video interview to decide whether an applicant advances to an in-person interview must collect specified race and ethnicity data for applicants advanced and not advanced, and applicants hired. It must report the data to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity annually by December 31 for the 12-month period ending the previous November 30.

applies_to.conditions: Triggered only when the employer relies solely on AI video analysis to decide whether an applicant will receive an in-person interview; this is narrower than ordinary AI-assisted video screening.

evidence: Demographic-data collection protocol and annual reporting dataset
DCEO filing receipt for the December 31 report

obligations.title: Keep licensed professionals responsible for AI-assisted therapy
obligations.plain: A licensed professional may use AI only for administrative or supplementary support while retaining full responsibility for interactions, outputs, and data use. If AI supplementary support records or transcribes a therapeutic session, the client or legally authorized representative must receive written notice of the AI use and its specific purpose and give consent.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to licensed professionals providing therapy or psychotherapy; the Act excludes religious counseling and peer support and has other specified exceptions.

evidence: Clinical workflow assigning full responsibility to the licensed professional
Written client notice, stated AI purpose, and consent for recorded/transcribed sessions

obligations.title: Do not let AI provide independent therapy
obligations.plain: Therapy or psychotherapy services offered to the Illinois public, including through internet-based AI, must be conducted by a licensed professional. A licensed professional may not allow AI to make independent therapeutic decisions, directly engage in therapeutic communication, generate recommendations or treatment plans without professional review and approval, or detect emotions or mental states.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to therapy or psychotherapy services offered to the public in Illinois; religious counseling, peer support, and other statutory exceptions are excluded.

evidence: Service design and clinical review controls showing no autonomous therapy or direct therapeutic communication
Approval records for AI-generated recommendations or treatment plans

obligations.title: Protect biometric data throughout its lifecycle
obligations.plain: A private entity possessing biometrics must publish a retention/destruction policy, give written notice of collection and purpose/term and obtain a written release before obtaining biometrics, limit disclosure and prohibit selling or profiting from the data, and protect it at least as carefully as other confidential sensitive information. The statute covers AI only when the data and activity meet BIPA's biometric definitions and private-entity scope.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to private entities collecting, receiving, possessing, or otherwise handling statutory biometric identifiers or information, such as scans of face or hand geometry, fingerprints, iris/retina scans, or voiceprints; statutory exclusions apply.

evidence: Public retention/destruction policy and pre-collection written notice/release
Access, disclosure, security, and destruction records for biometric data
obligations.notes: BIPA is a general biometric privacy statute, not an AI-specific rule; a facial image alone is not automatically a statutory face-geometry scan or biometric information. Public entities are outside the private-entity definition.

obligations.title: Establish and independently audit a frontier AI framework
obligations.plain: Beginning January 1, 2028, a large frontier developer must publish, implement, and annually review a framework for catastrophic-risk thresholds, mitigation, deployment decisions, third-party evaluation, cybersecurity, incident response, governance, and internal-use risks. It must also obtain an annual independent audit of Section 10 compliance beginning January 1, 2028 or 90 days after first qualifying as a large frontier developer, whichever is later.

applies_to.conditions: Frontier model means a foundation model trained with more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; large frontier developer means affiliate-inclusive annual gross revenue over $500 million in the preceding calendar year.

evidence: Published frontier AI framework and annual review/change records
Independent audit report, auditor-independence record, and remediation plan
obligations.notes: The audit starts January 1, 2028 or 90 days after a developer first qualifies as large, whichever is later; framework publication starts January 1, 2028.
obligations.instrument_short: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act
obligations.cite: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act §§5, 10(a)-(b), 10(d)

obligations.title: Publish frontier-model transparency reports
obligations.plain: Before or concurrently with deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model, a frontier developer must conspicuously publish a report with the developer's site and contact mechanism, release date, supported languages and output modalities, intended uses, and generally applicable use restrictions. A large frontier developer must add machine-readable summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments, results, third-party evaluators, and framework-compliance steps.

applies_to.conditions: The basic report applies to frontier developers; additional risk-assessment summaries apply to large frontier developers. Statutory New York-like thresholds are not prerequisites to the Illinois report beyond the Act's frontier-model definition and scope.

evidence: Published report or model/system card containing required information
Machine-readable assessment summaries and evaluator records, if large frontier developer
obligations.instrument_short: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act
obligations.cite: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act §10(c)(1)-(4)

obligations.title: Report catastrophic risks from internal model use
obligations.plain: A large frontier developer must send the Agency a summary of each catastrophic-risk assessment resulting from internal use of its frontier models every three months, or on another reasonable written schedule agreed with the Agency and communicated to the Attorney General with updates.

applies_to.conditions: Large frontier developers only; affiliate-inclusive annual gross revenue over $500 million in the preceding calendar year.

evidence: Internal-use catastrophic-risk assessment summaries
Submission receipts and written alternate schedule/update records
obligations.instrument_short: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act
obligations.cite: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act §10(e)

obligations.title: Report critical safety incidents within statutory windows
obligations.plain: A frontier developer must report a critical safety incident to the Agency and Attorney General within 72 hours after learning facts sufficient for a reasonable belief that one occurred. If the developer discovers imminent risk of death or serious physical injury, it must also disclose the incident within 24 hours to an appropriate authority with jurisdiction.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to critical safety incidents involving one or more frontier models; 24-hour reporting is triggered by imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

evidence: Incident record, classification rationale, and timestamped escalation decision
Agency, Attorney General, and emergency-authority submission receipts
obligations.instrument_short: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act
obligations.cite: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act §15(c)

obligations.title: File and maintain the large-developer disclosure
obligations.plain: Beginning January 1, 2027, a large frontier developer may not develop, deploy, or operate a frontier model wholly or partly in Illinois without a current disclosure statement filed with the Agency and payment of the required fee. The statement must be renewed annually and earlier after specified ownership or material-information changes.

applies_to.conditions: Large frontier developers only; specified ownership, Illinois-office, and regulatory-contact information must be disclosed, subject to the Act's filing terms.

evidence: Filed disclosure statement and annual/triggered updates
Agency fee payment and filing confirmation
obligations.penalty: After notice and hearing, $1,000 per day for specified filing failures plus unpaid assessments.
obligations.instrument_short: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act
obligations.cite: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act §18(a)-(f)

obligations.title: Protect covered employees who report safety concerns
obligations.plain: Frontier developers may not prevent or retaliate against covered employees who make specified good-faith disclosures, and must give covered employees clear notice of their rights. Large frontier developers must provide an anonymous internal reporting process with monthly status updates to reporters and share process disclosures/responses with officers and directors at least quarterly, subject to the statutory exception for implicated officers or directors.

applies_to.conditions: Covered employees are employees responsible for assessing, managing, or addressing critical-safety-incident risk; the anonymous internal process and quarterly sharing duties apply to large frontier developers.

evidence: Covered-employee rights notice and anti-retaliation policy
Anonymous reporting channel, monthly reporter updates, and quarterly board/officer records
obligations.notes: The Section 20 duties are effective on the Act's general January 1, 2027 date; do not treat the separately enacted IDHR employment rule proposal as operative.
obligations.instrument_short: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act
obligations.cite: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act §20(a)-(e)

obligations.title: Complete an independent bias audit before use
obligations.plain: An employer or employment agency may not use a covered AEDT to screen candidates for hiring or employees for promotion in New York City unless an independent auditor has completed a bias audit no more than one year before the tool's use. The audit must meet the rule's requirements for the tool and the employer's reliance on the audit.

applies_to.conditions: An AEDT is a computational process that substantially assists or replaces discretionary decision-making for hiring or promotion in NYC; limited standard-technology and non-substantial-use exclusions apply.

evidence: Independent auditor's dated bias-audit report for the specific AEDT
Audit scope and independence records showing the audit is no more than one year old at use

obligations.title: Calculate and document required audit metrics
obligations.plain: The audit must calculate selection or scoring rates and impact ratios for sex, race/ethnicity, and intersectional categories, and address unknown-category counts as required by the rule. It generally must use historical data; test data is permitted when historical data is insufficient for a statistically significant audit, with the required explanation in the summary.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to the independent bias audit for each covered AEDT; the 6 RCNY rule governs categories, data sufficiency, and reporting.

evidence: Audit calculations for selection/scoring rates, impact ratios, and unknown categories
Historical-data provenance or test-data sufficiency rationale and report

obligations.title: Publish the audit summary and tool distribution date
obligations.plain: Before using an AEDT, the employer or employment agency must make the date and summary of the most recent bias audit publicly available on its website. The information must remain posted until at least six months after the AEDT's last use.

applies_to.conditions: Covered AEDT use to screen candidates for hiring or employees for promotion in NYC.

evidence: Public audit summary and date of the most recent audit
Website publication and removal-date records

obligations.title: Give advance notice before using an AEDT
obligations.plain: The employer or employment agency must notify each NYC-resident candidate or employee at least 10 business days before using an AEDT to assess that person. Notice may be provided in a job posting or by mail or email as allowed by the DCWP guidance.

applies_to.conditions: Candidates or employees who are residents of New York City and are being assessed for hiring or promotion with a covered AEDT.

evidence: Dated notice or job posting showing the AEDT notice was provided at least 10 business days before use
Delivery record for each affected candidate or employee

obligations.title: Explain what the tool assesses and available options
obligations.plain: The advance notice must state that an AEDT will be used and identify the job qualifications and characteristics it will assess. It must also explain how the person can request an alternative selection process or accommodation.

applies_to.conditions: Same notice trigger and affected NYC-resident candidates or employees as §20-871(b)(2).

evidence: Notice template naming the AEDT and assessed qualifications/characteristics
Written instructions for requesting an alternative selection process or accommodation

obligations.title: Disclose AEDT data sources and retention policy
obligations.plain: If the information is not already disclosed on the employment section of the website, the employer or employment agency must provide, upon written request, the type and source of data collected by the AEDT and its data-retention policy within 30 days. If disclosure is withheld because it would violate law or interfere with a law-enforcement investigation, the employer must explain why.

applies_to.conditions: A candidate or employee may request this information in connection with the employer's covered AEDT use; statutory legal and law-enforcement exceptions apply.

evidence: Public employment-page disclosure or written-request procedure
Dated response within 30 days, or documented statutory exception and explanation

obligations.article: GBL §1421(1)-(2), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026
obligations.title: Publish and maintain a frontier AI framework
obligations.plain: A large frontier developer must write, implement, follow, and publish a frontier AI framework addressing catastrophic-risk assessment and mitigation, deployment review, cybersecurity, incident response, governance, and risks from internal use. It must review the framework at least annually and publish material changes with a justification within 30 days.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to frontier models developed, deployed, or operating wholly or partly in New York, subject to statutory exceptions. A frontier model exceeds 10^26 integer or floating-point operations; a large frontier developer has affiliate-inclusive annual gross revenue over $500 million in the preceding calendar year.

evidence: Current published frontier AI framework and annual review record
Change log and publication record for material framework revisions
obligations.penalty: Up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for a later violation under the Act's enforcement provision.
obligations.notes: Chapter 96 replaces the original Chapter 699 Article 44-B; all developer duties in the amended text take effect January 1, 2027. The first January 1, 2028 annual report is an Office duty; no independent developer audit mandate appears in the final New York text.
obligations.cite: RAISE Act GBL §1421(1)-(2), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026

obligations.article: GBL §1421(3), (5)-(6), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026
obligations.title: Publish frontier-model transparency reports
obligations.plain: Before or concurrently with deployment of a new or substantially modified frontier model, a frontier developer must publish a transparency report describing the model's release, supported languages and output modalities, intended uses, restrictions, and a developer contact mechanism. Large frontier developers must add summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments and related evaluation steps; permitted redactions require a public description and justification, and unredacted information must be retained for five years.

applies_to.conditions: Frontier-model and New York territorial thresholds apply; the additional risk-assessment summaries apply only to large frontier developers.

evidence: Published predeployment report or system/model card containing the required information
Redaction justification and five-year unredacted-retention record, if redactions are made
obligations.cite: RAISE Act GBL §1421(3), (5)-(6), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026

obligations.article: GBL §1422(2), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026
obligations.title: Submit internal-use catastrophic-risk summaries
obligations.plain: A large frontier developer must transmit the Office a summary of each assessment of catastrophic risk resulting from internal use of its frontier models every three months, or on another reasonable schedule that it specifies in writing to the Office and Attorney General and updates as appropriate with the Office's agreement.

applies_to.conditions: Large frontier developers only; affiliate-inclusive annual gross revenue over $500 million in the preceding calendar year.

evidence: Internal-use catastrophic-risk assessment summaries
Submission receipts and written schedule/updates agreed with the Office
obligations.cite: RAISE Act GBL §1422(2), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026

obligations.article: GBL §1422(3), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026
obligations.title: Report critical safety incidents on time
obligations.plain: A frontier developer must report a critical safety incident to the Office within 72 hours after determining that it occurred or learning facts sufficient for a reasonable belief that it occurred. If the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury, the developer must also disclose it within 24 hours to an appropriate authority with jurisdiction, as required by law.

applies_to.conditions: Critical safety incidents concerning frontier models within the Act's New York scope; the 24-hour duty is triggered by discovery of imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

evidence: Incident triage record showing the knowledge/determination timestamp and statutory classification
Copies and submission receipts for Office and emergency-authority reports
obligations.cite: RAISE Act GBL §1422(3), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026

obligations.article: GBL §1428(1)-(4), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026
obligations.title: File the large-developer disclosure and pay assessments
obligations.plain: A large frontier developer may not develop, deploy, or operate a frontier model wholly or partly in New York without a current disclosure statement filed with the Office and payment of its required share of administration costs. The statement must be renewed at least every two years and earlier after specified ownership or material-information changes.

applies_to.conditions: Large frontier developers only, subject to statutory exceptions; registration disclosures include developer identity, New York offices, specified ownership information, and regulatory contacts.

evidence: Filed disclosure statement and renewal/change submissions
Fee or assessment payment records
obligations.penalty: Daily civil penalties and unpaid assessments may be imposed after notice and hearing for specified filing failures.
obligations.cite: RAISE Act GBL §1428(1)-(4), as enacted by Chapter 96 of 2026

obligations.title: Detect and respond to self-harm signals
obligations.plain: An operator may provide a qualifying AI companion only if it has a protocol using reasonable efforts to detect and address users' expressions of suicidal ideation or self-harm. When such an expression is detected, the protocol must notify the user and refer them to crisis services, including 9-8-8 or another appropriate service.
