applies_to.conditions: Covers an AI system designed to simulate a sustained human-like relationship through retained interaction/preferences, unsolicited emotion-based questions, and ongoing dialogue about personal matters; statutory customer-service, efficiency/research/technical-assistance, and internal-use exclusions apply.

evidence: Safety protocol and test records for detecting and addressing suicidal ideation or self-harm
User-facing crisis referral shown when the relevant signal is detected

obligations.title: Remind users that a companion is not human
obligations.plain: An operator must give a clear and conspicuous notice at the beginning of an AI-companion interaction, no more than once per day, and at least every three hours during continuing interactions. The notice must say verbally or in writing that the user is not communicating with a human.

applies_to.conditions: Same Article 47 definition and statutory exclusions as §1701.

evidence: Product screenshots or interaction transcripts showing the beginning and recurring notices
Release test confirming the notice frequency and accessible presentation

obligations.title: Disclose personalized algorithmic prices
obligations.plain: An entity that sets the price of a specific good or service using personalized algorithmic pricing and advertises or otherwise presents that price to a New York consumer using personal data specific to that consumer must display the prescribed clear and conspicuous disclosure: “THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA”. The statute requires disclosure; it does not prohibit personalized algorithmic pricing.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to covered New York entities and consumer-facing prices set dynamically by an algorithm using personal data; statutory definitions and exceptions apply. The law regulates algorithmic pricing, not only AI systems.

evidence: Price-page or offer screenshots showing the disclosure in the required proximity and timing
Pricing-system configuration and data-source record showing whether the statutory trigger is met
obligations.notes: The statute became effective July 8, 2025; the Attorney General announced enforcement beginning November 10, 2025 after a litigation-related pause. Do not treat proposed broader prohibitions as enacted law.

obligations.title: Maintain and publish the State AI inventory
obligations.plain: The Office of Information Technology Services must maintain and publish an annual inventory of State-agency AI systems, including information such as purpose and uses. State agencies must submit requested inventory data at least 60 days before the annual December 30 publication date; specified security-sensitive information may be withheld.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to State agencies and AI systems meeting the statute's definition, including systems that may directly impact the public; basic calculations, basic automation, and specified rule-based systems are excluded.

evidence: Current AI-system inventory record with purpose, use, and required data elements
Submission receipt and security-based withholding rationale, if applicable

obligations.title: Publish State-agency employment-tool lists
obligations.plain: A State agency using an automated employment decision-making tool must publish a list on its website by December 30 following the applicable effective date and annually thereafter. The list must describe each tool, state when agency use began, and summarize its purpose and use.

applies_to.conditions: State-agency tools that materially automate or replace human employment decision-making; the statutory definition excludes basic computerized processes that do not materially affect an individual's rights, liberties, benefits, safety, or welfare.

evidence: Public agency AEDT list with description, start date, and purpose/use summary
Publication and annual-update records

obligations.title: Publish covered-entity employment-tool lists
obligations.plain: To the extent feasible, each covered entity using an automated employment decision-making tool must publish an annual website list describing the tool, when use began, and its purpose and use. Covered entities include counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts, BOCES, specified district corporations, SUNY, CUNY, and community colleges.

applies_to.conditions: To the extent feasible; first list is due December 30, 2027 for the provision added by Chapter 86 of 2026.

evidence: Public covered-entity AEDT list with description, start date, and purpose/use summary
Annual publication records

obligations.article: Civil Service Law §80(10), as amended by Chapter 86 of 2026
obligations.title: Preserve public employees' existing rights and duties
obligations.plain: Use of a covered State AI system may not displace or reduce specified public employees, transfer their existing duties to AI, impair existing collective-bargaining agreements, or alter protected employment rights and status. The provisions apply to the public employers and employee groups identified in the amended statute and expire July 1, 2028.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to AI systems defined by State Technology Law §103-e and the covered public-sector employees/entities specified in the statute; the provision is scheduled to expire July 1, 2028.

evidence: Workforce-impact and duty-allocation review for covered AI deployments
Collective-bargaining and employee-rights compliance records
obligations.notes: Chapter 86 repealed the earlier impact-assessment and meaningful-human-review framework before it became operative; this entry covers surviving inventory, disclosure, and workforce provisions only.
obligations.cite: LOADinG Act Civil Service Law §80(10), as amended by Chapter 86 of 2026

obligations.title: Gate unsafe companion features by age
obligations.plain: An operator may not provide unsafe features through a covered generative-AI system with a natural-language interface and ongoing adaptive responses unless the user is not a covered minor and the operator uses an age-assurance method permitted under Article 45 and its rules. Unsafe features include portraying the AI as a living or human character, relationship or authority figure; personal opinions or emotional appeals; flattery or unsolicited emotional probes; use of personal/health information from more than 12 hours earlier or a prior session; deceptive companionship; suicide, self-harm, eating-disorder or substance-misuse content; secrecy, isolation or discouraging help-seeking; engagement overriding safety guardrails; and sexually explicit or child-sexual-abuse content. Statutory customer-service, efficiency/research/technical-assistance, and internal-use exceptions apply.

applies_to.conditions: A covered user is a user of a covered AI companion in New York who is not the operator or its agent/affiliate. A covered minor is a user whom the operator actually knows is under 18; the prohibition still requires the operator to use permitted age-assurance methods before providing unsafe features.

evidence: Feature-level safety tests and release-blocking rules for the enumerated categories
Age-assurance decision record showing the permitted method and result
obligations.notes: Final Assembly bill text and current Senate codification state January 1, 2027; Senator Kristen Gonzalez's October 30, 2026 press release says the signed chaptered version changed the date to June 1, 2027. The signed Chapter 368 text/Approval Memo 6 was not independently retrieved, so the effective date remains contested; this record follows the available final bill text and codification pending confirmation.
obligations.instrument_short: Unsafe AI Companion Features for Minors
obligations.cite: Unsafe AI Companion Features for Minors GBL §§1800(5), 1800(8)-(12), 1801(1)-(2)

obligations.title: Use privacy-preserving age assurance
obligations.plain: Until the referenced Attorney General or Article 45 age-assurance rules apply, an operator must use a reasonable method that guards against circumvention and minimizes retention, offer more than one method (including one that avoids government ID or preserves anonymity), and may rely on self-declaration only when the user declares minor status. Age-assurance information may be used only to determine minor status and must be deleted immediately after the attempt, subject to legal-retention exceptions.

applies_to.conditions: Operators of covered AI companions providing unsafe features under Article 48; statutory exceptions and applicable future regulations may alter the interim methods.

evidence: Age-assurance method inventory and evidence that multiple options are offered
Data-flow, purpose-limitation, and immediate-deletion test records
obligations.notes: The Article 48 effective-date conflict described in the §1801 obligation also affects this phase-in.
obligations.instrument_short: Unsafe AI Companion Features for Minors
obligations.cite: Unsafe AI Companion Features for Minors GBL §1804(1)-(3)

obligations.title: Do not intentionally incite self-harm, violence, or crime
obligations.plain: A person may not develop or deploy an AI system in a manner that intentionally aims to incite or encourage a person to commit physical self-harm (including suicide), harm another person, or engage in criminal activity. The prohibition turns on the specified intent, not merely on a harmful outcome.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to persons within the Texas scope in § 551.002; the conduct must intentionally aim to incite or encourage one of the listed acts.

evidence: Use-case and policy screening against the statutory intent-based prohibition
Safety testing and review records for system behavior and reported misuse
obligations.penalty: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000-$40,000 per day for a continuing violation, subject to the statutory cure and enforcement provisions.
obligations.notes: The Act does not establish a general duty to assess disparate impact or a general appeal right for consequential decisions.

obligations.title: Do not use AI for prohibited government social scoring
obligations.plain: A governmental entity may not use or deploy AI to evaluate or classify people based on known, inferred, or predicted social behavior or personal characteristics with intent to assign a social score that results or may result in specified detrimental or disproportionate treatment, or infringement of rights under the U.S. or Texas Constitution or other law.

applies_to.conditions: Only governmental entities; the statute requires intent to assign a score and one of the listed harmful or rights-infringing consequences.

evidence: Public-sector AI use-case review and written social-scoring prohibition
System-purpose documentation and audit records for categorization or scoring tools
obligations.penalty: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000-$40,000 per day for a continuing violation, subject to the statutory cure and enforcement provisions.

obligations.title: Limit government biometric identification that infringes rights
obligations.plain: A governmental entity may not develop or deploy AI to uniquely identify a specific individual using biometric data, or targeted or untargeted gathering of publicly available images or other media, without consent when the gathering would infringe a right protected by the U.S. or Texas Constitution or other state or federal law. Section 503.001 also restricts commercial biometric capture, with statutory exceptions for certain AI training and security or fraud-prevention uses.

applies_to.conditions: Government biometric-identification restriction applies only when the specified gathering would infringe a legal right; statutory definitions and § 503.001 exceptions apply.

evidence: Biometric data inventory, purpose and consent records, and rights-impact review for government uses
Documentation that any relied-on § 503.001 exception applies and that later commercial use is handled under that section
obligations.penalty: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000-$40,000 per day for a continuing violation, subject to the statutory cure and enforcement provisions.
obligations.notes: The statute is not a blanket ban on all biometric AI or public-source media; its government-use restriction includes a rights-infringement condition. Section 503.001 has additional definitions and exceptions.
obligations.cite: Texas TRAIGA Bus. & Com. Code § 552.054 and § 503.001

obligations.title: Do not target constitutional rights or unlawfully discriminate by intent
obligations.plain: A person may not develop or deploy AI with the sole intent to infringe, restrict, or impair an individual's U.S. constitutional rights, or with intent to unlawfully discriminate against a protected class in violation of state or federal law. Disparate impact alone is not sufficient to prove the discrimination intent; statutory insurance and federally insured financial-institution provisions apply.

applies_to.conditions: The constitutional-rights prohibition uses a sole-intent standard; the discrimination prohibition requires intent and violation of other state or federal law, with express financial and insurance provisions.

evidence: Documented use-case and policy review against the statutory intent-based prohibitions
Review of insurance or federally insured bank treatment where an exception is claimed
obligations.penalty: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000-$40,000 per day for a continuing violation, subject to the statutory cure and enforcement provisions.
obligations.notes: The statute does not make disparate impact alone sufficient to prove intent. The § 552.056 exemptions/constructive-compliance provisions are limited to specified insurance entities and federally insured financial institutions complying with applicable laws.

obligations.title: Do not develop specified AI sexual-abuse material or child-impersonating chat
obligations.plain: A person may not develop or distribute an AI system with the sole intent to produce, assist in producing, or distribute visual material that violates the Texas child-pornography statute or deepfake videos/images that violate Penal Code § 21.165. A person also may not intentionally develop or distribute an AI system that has text-based sexual-conduct conversations while impersonating or imitating a child under 18.

applies_to.conditions: The visual-material prohibition uses the statute's sole-intent standard and Penal Code references; the child-impersonating chat prohibition uses its separate intentional-development/distribution standard.

evidence: Model and content-policy tests for the specified statutory content and child-impersonation scenarios
Incident-handling and distribution controls for prohibited outputs or system behavior
obligations.penalty: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000-$40,000 per day for a continuing violation, subject to the statutory cure and enforcement provisions.
obligations.notes: This is not a general prohibition on every AI-generated sexual image; the statute ties the visual-material prohibition to specified Texas Penal Code violations and intent.

obligations.title: Disclose government AI interactions to consumers
obligations.plain: A governmental agency that makes available an AI system intended to interact with consumers must clearly and conspicuously disclose, before or at the time of interaction, that the consumer is interacting with AI. The notice must be in plain language and not use a dark pattern; it is required even when AI use would be obvious, and may be provided through a hyperlink.

applies_to.conditions: Applies to a governmental agency's AI system intended to interact with consumers; the Act does not create a general private-company chatbot disclosure rule.

evidence: Screenshots or transcripts showing clear, plain-language disclosure before or at first interaction
Review records showing the disclosure does not use a dark pattern
obligations.penalty: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000-$40,000 per day for a continuing violation, subject to the statutory cure and enforcement provisions.

obligations.title: Disclose AI use in health-care services or treatment
obligations.plain: If an AI system is used in relation to a health-care service or treatment, the provider must disclose the AI interaction to the recipient or personal representative no later than the date the service or treatment is first provided. In an emergency, disclosure must be made as soon as reasonably possible; the disclosure is subject to the section's plain-language, clear-and-conspicuous, and no-dark-pattern requirements.

applies_to.conditions: Licensed, registered, or certified provider uses an AI system in relation to health-care service or treatment; emergency timing exception applies.

evidence: Patient notice or form documenting AI use, delivery date, and recipient or personal representative
Emergency procedure documenting disclosure as soon as reasonably possible
obligations.penalty: $10,000-$12,000 per curable violation; $80,000-$200,000 per uncurable violation; $2,000-$40,000 per day for a continuing violation, subject to the statutory cure and enforcement provisions.

obligations.title: Apply and report if participating in the AI regulatory sandbox
obligations.plain: A sandbox applicant must obtain approval from the Department of Information Resources and each applicable agency before testing and submit the system description and intended use, a benefit assessment addressing consumer, privacy, and public-safety impacts, a mitigation plan, and proof of applicable federal AI-law compliance. Approved participants may test and deploy for up to 36 months (extendable for good cause) and must report quarterly on performance, risk mitigation, and consumer/stakeholder feedback; Chapter 552 duties and prohibitions cannot be waived.

applies_to.conditions: Only persons who voluntarily apply for and are approved as sandbox participants; approval by DIR and any applicable agency is required before testing under the program.

evidence: Approved sandbox application, benefit assessment, federal-law proof, and mitigation plan
Quarterly reports to DIR covering performance, risks, and consumer or stakeholder feedback
obligations.penalty: Sandbox relief does not waive Chapter 552 duties or prohibitions; other penalties depend on the law or regulation at issue.
obligations.notes: The impact/benefit assessment is a condition only for sandbox participation, not a general TRAIGA assessment duty for all developers or deployers.

obligations.title: Designate a Chief AI Officer
obligations.plain: The head of each covered agency must retain or designate a Chief AI Officer to promote agency AI innovation, adoption, and governance. An existing senior official may serve if they have significant AI expertise and the authority and access required by the memorandum.

applies_to.conditions: Covered executive-branch agencies; the memorandum excludes AI used as a component of a national security system and contains additional agency-specific exceptions.

evidence: Agency designation memo naming the CAIO and defining their authority and responsibilities
obligations.notes: The 60-day designation deadline was 2025-06-02. M-25-21 is an internal federal policy and does not create private-sector duties.

obligations.title: Maintain and publish annual AI use-case inventories
obligations.plain: Covered agencies must inventory AI use cases at least annually, submit the inventory to OMB, and publish a public version on the agency website. The public-inventory requirement does not apply to the Department of Defense or Intelligence Community; other stated agency and national-security exceptions also apply.

applies_to.conditions: Covered agencies under M-25-21; DoD and Intelligence Community are excluded from the public version of the inventory.

evidence: Dated agency AI use-case inventory and OMB submission record
Public inventory page or documented exception for non-public inventories

obligations.title: Apply minimum risk practices to high-impact AI
obligations.plain: Agencies must conduct pre-deployment testing, prepare risk-mitigation plans, and complete a documented AI impact assessment before deploying a high-impact use case; they must periodically update the assessment and monitor performance and risks. Agencies must discontinue or cease use when the system fails the required practices and the risks cannot be mitigated.

applies_to.conditions: High-impact AI is AI whose output is a principal basis for a decision or action with legal, material, binding, or significant effects on rights or safety; M-25-21 has national-security-system and specified agency exceptions and limited pilot provisions.

evidence: Pre-deployment test results, risk-mitigation plan, and signed AI impact assessment
Periodic monitoring records and documented stop-use or remediation decisions
obligations.notes: Agencies had 365 days, through 2026-04-03, to document implementation of the minimum practices.

obligations.title: Put required safeguards into covered AI contracts
obligations.plain: For covered solicitations and later contract options, agencies must include appropriate terms addressing privacy, government data and intellectual-property rights, M-25-21 high-impact AI requirements, and the agency's ability to conduct ongoing testing and monitoring. AI systems operated as agency information systems also need an authorization to operate before deployment.

applies_to.conditions: Covered executive-branch agency acquisitions of AI systems or services under solicitations issued on or after 2025-09-30, and options exercised after that date; excludes Intelligence Community elements and AI acquired for use in a national security system.

evidence: Solicitation and contract clauses covering privacy, government data/IP, high-impact AI practices, and testing access
Authorization-to-operate decision and contract monitoring records where applicable
obligations.notes: M-25-22 includes recommendations as well as mandatory requirements; this entry lists the stated mandatory contract terms, not optional vendor-lock-in practices.

obligations.title: Procure LLMs developed under the Unbiased AI Principles
obligations.plain: Agency heads must procure only LLMs developed in accordance with the order's truth-seeking and ideological-neutrality principles. The order concerns federal procurement and does not impose a general private-market model-design mandate.

applies_to.conditions: Federal agency procurement of LLMs; national-security-system exceptions may be provided in OMB guidance.

evidence: Procurement evaluation documenting the principles and the agency's review of vendor information
obligations.notes: OMB implemented the order through M-26-04; its contract and policy requirements are listed separately.

obligations.title: Include Unbiased AI Principles in LLM procurement
obligations.plain: Agencies must put contractual requirements addressing the Unbiased AI Principles in post-11 December 2025 solicitations or orders for LLM procurement, obtain enough vendor information to assess compliance, and update procurement policies and user-feedback procedures by 11 March 2026. The memo also sets a two-year sunset unless extended by OMB.

applies_to.conditions: Covered agencies procuring LLMs; excludes national security systems, with specified factors for applying the requirements to agency-developed LLMs and non-LLM models.

evidence: LLM solicitation and contract clauses requiring compliance with the principles
Agency procurement policy and user process for reporting outputs that may violate the principles
obligations.notes: This memo governs agency procurement; it is not a generally applicable private-sector AI standard and is scheduled to sunset 2027-12-11 unless extended.

obligations.title: Use the prescribed term in future federal AI communications
obligations.plain: To the maximum extent permitted by law, executive departments and agencies must use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” instead of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory executive-branch documents. The order does not require altering statutes, prior regulations, contracts, or historical documents.

applies_to.conditions: Non-statutory executive-branch communications and documents issued after the order; subject to applicable law.

evidence: Current agency style guidance and a review process for covered non-statutory documents
obligations.notes: Terminology rule for federal agencies only. No governance control in the shared vocabulary maps to it, so controls is empty on purpose.

obligations.title: Do not knowingly publish specified nonconsensual intimate depictions
obligations.plain: In interstate or foreign commerce, it is unlawful to use an interactive computer service to knowingly publish certain intimate visual depictions of identifiable adults or minors without consent, including covered digital forgeries made with AI. The adult and minor offenses have different intent or harm conditions and statutory exceptions.

applies_to.conditions: Applies only to the statutory categories and circumstances in 47 U.S.C. §223(h), including the separate rules for adult and minor subjects and the listed exceptions.

evidence: Content policy prohibiting covered nonconsensual intimate depictions and escalation records for suspected violations

obligations.title: Provide notice and remove validly reported intimate depictions
obligations.plain: Covered platforms must provide a clear, plain-language notice of a removal process for intimate depictions published without consent, including AI digital forgeries. After a valid request, the platform must remove the depiction and make reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies as soon as possible and no later than 48 hours.

applies_to.conditions: Covered platforms as defined by the Act; removal duties concern intimate visual depictions published on the platform without the identifiable person's consent.

evidence: Clear notice and functioning request channel, including for people without platform accounts
Takedown timestamps, disposition records, and reasonable-efforts records for known identical copies
obligations.penalty: A failure to reasonably comply is treated as an FTC Act violation; FTC guidance states potential civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation.
obligations.notes: The one-year compliance deadline ran from enactment on 2025-05-19. The FTC began enforcement on 2026-05-19.

obligations.title: Do not make deceptive AI claims to consumers
obligations.plain: The FTC Act's existing prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce applies to AI-related marketing and conduct. Companies must not make deceptive claims about AI capabilities or use AI to facilitate deception; the law does not create a general warranty that every AI output is accurate.

applies_to.conditions: Conduct in or affecting commerce within the FTC's jurisdiction; statutory exceptions and other applicable law remain relevant.

evidence: Substantiation for material performance, accuracy, earnings, or professional-service claims about AI products
Review records for AI-enabled marketing and consumer-facing representations
obligations.notes: FTC's Operation AI Comply is an enforcement example, not a new AI-specific rule. The FTC's June 2026 AI-accuracy policy statement was proposed for comment, not a final rule.

obligations.title: Establish a DoD-wide AI and ML cybersecurity policy
obligations.plain: The Secretary of Defense must develop and implement a department-wide policy for cybersecurity and associated governance of AI and machine-learning systems, applications, and models used in national-defense applications. The policy must address AI-specific threats, lifecycle safeguards, testing, auditing, monitoring, and workforce training.

applies_to.conditions: Department of Defense systems, applications, and models used in national-defense applications.

evidence: Published or approved DoD AI/ML security and governance policy
Implementation records for lifecycle security, testing, monitoring, and workforce training
obligations.notes: Section 1512 set a 180-day policy deadline of 2026-06-16 and required a report to the congressional armed-services committees by 2026-08-31.

obligations.title: Develop DoD AI security requirements for covered entities
obligations.plain: The Secretary of Defense must develop a risk-based physical- and cybersecurity framework for covered AI/ML technologies and amend the DFARS or take similar action to require covered entities to implement it. A covered entity is a contractor or other entity developing, deploying, storing, or hosting covered AI/ML technology for DoD.

applies_to.conditions: This records DoD's statutory implementation duty; a company's specific requirements depend on an applicable DoD solicitation, contract clause, or similar action.

evidence: DoD AI security framework and implementation plan
Applicable DFARS clause or similar procurement action identifying contractor requirements
obligations.notes: Section 1513 separately required an implementation-status update to the congressional defense committees within 180 days of enactment.

obligations.title: Keep covered DeepSeek and High Flyer AI out of DoD contract performance
obligations.plain: DoD must require covered AI applications to be excluded from and removed from its systems and devices, and contractors may not use covered AI in performing a DoD contract. Covered AI includes models or successor models developed by DeepSeek or High Flyer and specified affiliated entities; the Secretary may grant case-specific waivers for listed research, evaluation, national-security, or mission-critical purposes with risk mitigation.

applies_to.conditions: Contractors during performance of a contract with the Department of Defense; statutory waiver exceptions and definitions apply.

evidence: Vendor and subcontractor AI-use screening for DoD contract performance
Documented waiver and risk-mitigation approval where an exception is used
obligations.notes: The 30-day deadline after enactment was 2026-01-17; the statutory restriction is limited to the covered AI defined in §1532.

obligations.title: Assess and oversee major DoD AI systems
obligations.plain: The Secretary of Defense must establish a cross-functional team to develop a standard AI model assessment framework and governance structure, designate functional leads, and assess major AI systems against the framework. A major system meets the statutory impact, user-count, and operational-use thresholds; systems used solely for undeployed research, development, testing, or evaluation are excluded.

applies_to.conditions: Department of Defense major AI systems meeting §1533(f)(3)'s criteria, including at least 500 annual DoD users and specified high-impact or operational conditions.

evidence: Team charter, assessment framework, and governance structure
Assessment records for major AI systems and documentation of use-case risk levels
obligations.notes: The statute set future deadlines for functional leads (2027-01-01), framework completion (2027-06-01), and major-system assessments (2028-01-01); the team-establishment deadline was 2026-06-01.

obligations.title: Require removal of DeepSeek from intelligence-community systems
obligations.plain: The Director of National Intelligence must issue standards and guidelines requiring removal of the DeepSeek application or successor service from national security systems operated by an intelligence-community element, its contractor, or another entity acting for it. The standards must include national-security and research exceptions with risk-mitigation requirements.

applies_to.conditions: Intelligence-community national security systems, including systems operated by contractors or other entities on behalf of an element.

evidence: DNI-issued standards and guidelines implementing the covered-application removal requirement
System and contractor screening records, including risk controls for approved exceptions
obligations.notes: The 60-day deadline to issue initial standards was 2026-02-16; §6604 requires standards and guidelines rather than stating an unrestricted direct prohibition on all DeepSeek use.

obligations.title: Do not use AI for prohibited or unlawful purposes
obligations.plain: The Law prohibits using AI to commit illegal acts or violate others' lawful interests; to systematically deceive or manipulate people through synthetic simulations of real persons or events where serious harm results; to exploit vulnerable groups to cause harm; or to create or spread falsified content capable of seriously harming national security, public order or social safety. It also prohibits unlawful data use, disabling required human oversight, and concealing or falsifying mandatory transparency information, labels or warnings.
evidence: Documented use-case screening against the prohibited purposes in Article 7
Controls and review records for required human oversight, labels and warnings
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.

obligations.title: Classify AI by risk and notify medium- and high-risk systems
obligations.plain: Providers must classify each AI system before putting it into use. The Law distinguishes high-, medium- and low-risk systems; providers must prepare classification dossiers and notify the Ministry of Science and Technology before service for medium- and high-risk systems. Deployers take over the provider's classification and must cooperate in reclassification when a deployment change, integration or modified function or purpose creates new or higher risk.

applies_to.conditions: Providers classify all systems; dossiers and advance notification apply to medium- and high-risk systems only.

evidence: Risk-classification rationale and dossier for each medium- or high-risk system
Ministry notification confirmation or system identifier, plus reclassification records where needed
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.notes: Decree 142 supplies dossier and filing details. It defines high-risk systems by the Prime Minister's list and sets medium-risk criteria; the system, rather than a model alone, is classified. Article 46 of the Decree provides an alternative official reporting channel if the national portal is not yet operational.
obligations.cite: Vietnam AI Law Art. 9-10; Decree 142, Arts. 5-6, 11-12 and 14

obligations.title: Disclose AI interactions and machine-mark generated audio, images and video
obligations.plain: Providers must ensure that people interacting directly with an AI system are informed they are interacting with AI. Providers must also apply machine-readable technical marks to AI-generated or edited audio, image and video outputs, using a method permitted by the Decree and maintaining the marking through generation and export within the system's control.
evidence: First-interaction disclosure screenshot or transcript
Technical description and detection tests for machine-readable marking on audio, image and video outputs
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.notes: Decree 142, effective 1 May 2026, specifies that machine-readable marking is not required for text output unless another law provides otherwise. It permits file-structure or metadata marks, digital/electronic signatures, or another machine-recognizable technical method.
obligations.cite: Vietnam AI Law Art. 11(1)-(2); Decree 142, Art. 17

obligations.title: Notify the public and visibly label potentially misleading AI content
obligations.plain: Deployers must clearly notify the public when releasing AI-generated or edited text, audio, images or video that could confuse people about the authenticity of an event or person. They must visibly label AI audio, image or video that simulates a real person's appearance or voice, or recreates a real event, so it can be distinguished from authentic content.

applies_to.conditions: Public release; notification is required for content capable of causing confusion, and visible labels are required for the specified synthetic or recreated audio, image and video.

evidence: Published content examples showing a clear notice or label at or before first access
Publishing workflow identifying the responsible deployer and permitted exceptions
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.notes: Decree 142 allows exclusions from visible labeling for technical edits that do not change substance or context, specified text proofreading, summaries, paraphrases or translations that do not distort the original, internal-only content, and controlled research/testing not released publicly. Creative works may use an appropriate label in credits or accompanying material, provided the AI origin remains clear.
obligations.cite: Vietnam AI Law Art. 11(3)-(5); Decree 142, Art. 18

obligations.article: Art. 12 of the AI Law; Decree 142, Art. 19(2)-(8)
obligations.title: Contain and report serious AI incidents on time
obligations.plain: Developers and providers must promptly take technical measures to correct, suspend or recall a system and notify the competent authority; deployers and users must record incidents, limit harm and notify the provider. A provider, or a deployer unable to contact the provider, must make a preliminary report within 72 hours after confirming an urgent serious incident (including death or serious health harm, serious public service disruption or national-security effects, and uncontrolled rights harm); other serious incidents are due within five working days. A final remediation report is due within 15 days after the preliminary report.

applies_to.conditions: Only serious incidents as defined in the AI Law and Decree; the 72-hour deadline is not the deadline for every incident.

evidence: Incident runbook with confirmation triggers, 72-hour and five-working-day clocks, and 15-day follow-up
Incident logs and copies of preliminary and final reports or escalation notices
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.cite: AI Law Implementing Decree Art. 12 of the AI Law; Decree 142, Art. 19(2)-(8)

obligations.title: Assess conformity of high-risk AI before use and after significant changes
obligations.plain: Providers of high-risk systems must complete conformity assessment before putting the system into service and reassess after significant changes that affect the original result. Systems on the Prime Minister's list requiring mandatory certification need assessment by a registered or recognized conformity-assessment organization; other high-risk systems may be self-assessed by the provider or assessed by such an organization. Providers must maintain conformity and disclose assessment results as required by the Decree.

applies_to.conditions: Systems on the high-risk list; third-party certification is required only for systems specifically listed for mandatory certification.

evidence: Conformity-assessment report or certificate, change-trigger reassessment and maintained technical dossier
Public disclosure/portal record of the result, or the officially announced alternative channel
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.notes: Decision 33's high-risk list took effect on 15 August 2026. Existing systems and listed systems subject to transition have the staged dates recorded under the Law and Decision instruments; systems on the mandatory certification list require third-party assessment rather than self-assessment.
obligations.cite: Vietnam AI Law Art. 13; Decree 142, Art. 13; Decision 33/2026/QD-TTg

obligations.title: Manage high-risk systems with documented controls and human oversight
obligations.plain: Providers of high-risk systems must maintain risk-management measures, govern training, testing and operational data, keep technical dossiers and logs, design for human oversight and intervention, meet transparency and incident duties, and give deployers and affected people functional information, operating guidance and risk warnings without disclosing source code or protected business secrets. Deployers must use systems within their classified purpose and risk, monitor operation, protect data, enable human intervention, control emerging risks and cooperate with providers and authorities.

applies_to.conditions: Only systems classified as high-risk; users must also follow operating procedures and promptly notify deployers of incidents under Art. 14(3).

evidence: Risk-management file, data-governance records, system dossier and operating logs
Human-oversight procedures, deployer instructions, user warnings and monitoring records
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.notes: Existing systems may continue operating during their statutory transition unless authorities identify a risk of serious harm and require suspension or termination. See the 1 March 2027 and 1 September 2027 deadlines.
obligations.cite: Vietnam AI Law Art. 14(1)-(5); Decree 142, Art. 15

obligations.title: Foreign high-risk providers must maintain a Vietnam contact point
obligations.plain: A foreign provider whose high-risk AI system is provided in Vietnam must have a legal contact point in Vietnam. If the system is subject to mandatory conformity certification before it is put into service, the provider must also have a commercial presence or an authorized representative in Vietnam.

applies_to.conditions: Foreign providers of high-risk systems provided in Vietnam; the additional commercial-presence or authorized-representative requirement applies when mandatory pre-use certification is required.

evidence: Vietnam legal-contact details and evidence the contact point is maintained
Commercial-presence records or written authorized-representative mandate where certification is mandatory
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.notes: Article 2 applies to foreign organizations and individuals participating in AI activities in Vietnam. The exact reach to foreign services provided entirely offshore without other Vietnam activities is not expressly resolved by that wording.

obligations.article: Art. 27(3)-(4) of the AI Law; Decree 142, Art. 20
obligations.title: Assess public-sector AI impacts before qualifying use
obligations.plain: State agencies must prepare an impact-assessment report before using a high-risk AI system or a system whose output is directly used as the basis for an administrative decision. The report must identify and assess risks, state control and mitigation measures, and explain human oversight and intervention; agencies must publish it except for state secrets, business secrets and personal data, and reassess after relevant changes create new or changed risks.

applies_to.conditions: High-risk systems, or systems whose output directly supports an administrative decision; other public-sector systems may be covered if they significantly affect human rights, social equality or public interests under Art. 27(3).

evidence: Approved impact-assessment report identifying risks, controls and human-oversight measures
Public disclosure record and supplemental assessment where a relevant system change occurs
obligations.penalty: Administrative or criminal sanctions and civil compensation may apply under Article 29 and other laws; no AI-law fine cap is specified here.
obligations.cite: AI Law Implementing Decree Art. 27(3)-(4) of the AI Law; Decree 142, Art. 20

obligations.title: Protect personal data processed using AI
obligations.plain: Personal data in AI processing must be used for the stated purpose and limited to what is necessary, with appropriate security measures, authentication and access controls. Personal-data processing by AI must be classified by risk level so appropriate protections can be applied; the Law prohibits using or developing AI systems involving personal data to harm national defense, security, public order or safety, or another person's life, health, dignity, reputation or property.

applies_to.conditions: Applies when personal data are processed in AI systems or services, regardless of whether the system is otherwise classified high, medium or low risk.

evidence: AI personal-data risk classification and corresponding safeguards
Purpose/necessity records, security measures and authentication/access-control configuration
obligations.notes: Article 30 is AI-specific; other PDPL requirements, including data-subject rights and impact-assessment duties, may also apply depending on the processing. The separate five-year provisions for some smaller entities do not disapply Article 30.
